articles.title: Gavin Newsom won the argument on California’s proposed wealth tax. He could still face a fight over it
articles.summary: The downfall of a one-time wealth tax on billionaires in solidly Democratic California – during a blue wave election – is a sobering outcome for its advocate...
articles.body:
The downfall of a one-time wealth tax on billionaires in solidly Democratic California – during a blue wave election – is a sobering outcome for its advocates, including progressive leaders such as Sen. Bernie Sanders and home state Rep. Ro Khanna.

But it could also be a challenge for a prominent opponent, outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, as he eyes a potential 2028 presidential campaign. Newsom said he would vote against the measure , arguing that a single-state effort would only drive billionaires to other states and harm California's budget.

With Khanna himself weighing a White House bid, the policy split could animate a smoldering divide between progressives in the upcoming national campaign. Even while California voters overall rejected the wealth tax, exit polls showed that Democratic voters favored it by nearly two-to-one.

"The reason we didn't win is because of Newsom," said Khanna, who represents Silicon Valley in the House and has allied himself with Sanders. "He chose to align with Republican donors, Trump donors, instead of the California Democratic Party and the California labor movement. It was appalling."

Newsom's team declined to respond to Khanna, who accused Newsom of not wanting to "offend the billionaire donors whose money he wants to get … for running a campaign."

But a source familiar with the governor's thinking says Newsom views the results of the ballot initiative as an affirmation of his position rather than a future political liability.

The source argued he was comfortable bucking conventional wisdom, pointing to his early advocacy for legalizing gay marriage, and the more recent decision to commute the sentences of all 548 state death row prisoners to life without parole.

Newsom argued before the vote that he backed a "true minimum tax on billionaires" and closing loopholes at the national level, acknowledging the broader policy arguments and political priorities of the Democratic electorate.

Proponents, however, remain frustrated with his opposition to the wealth tax, and blamed him for the defeat.

"It turned out that in this election, the Democratic governor was on the side of billionaires and not on the side of health workers," said Brian Galle, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and one of the architects of the initiative. "It's very difficult, it turns out, to do progressive tax policy if you have a popular Democratic governor who's telling voters to do something different."

Advocates of the tax said it was a necessary response to federal healthcare spending cuts from Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act, estimating a shortfall of about $20 billion per year for California moving forward, which threatens the state's Medi-Cal program that provides healthcare to low-income Californians.

They estimated the wealth tax could have raised $100 billion, enough to cover the shortfall for about five years.

Opponents of the measure had argued it could harm the state where they built their businesses and fortunes, with Google co-founder Sergey Brin — who was born in Moscow — comparing the tax in a rare comment to The New York Times to the society he fled as a child and saying he doesn't want California to adopt socialism.

The wealth tax would have applied to around 250 billionaires in California, with the funding raised primarily earmarked for healthcare following federal cuts to Medicaid and other programs.

Tech and corporate leaders had threatened to move their residences, and even their businesses, out of California if the measure passed — potentially depriving the state of crucial jobs and tax revenue.

Brin was the largest backer of the opposition. He contributed $132 million, a huge sum for a state ballot initiative — but relatively small compared to up to $14 billion in potential tax liabilities he faced if it passed.

Brin's peers hailed his contributions to the wealth tax's projected defeat on social media posts. "We dodged a bullet on this asset seizure tax," wrote Garry Tan, the CEO of Y Combinator, an influential startup incubator. "Huge thanks to Sergey Brin here."

A cohort of other wealthy Californians also shelled out millions in the effort to block the tax, including venture capitalist Peter Thiel; John Doerr, chairman of the venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins; and Patrick Collison, CEO of the digital financial services company Stripe, according to campaign finance records.

Those millions funded rival ballot initiatives that could have superseded and invalidated the wealth tax, in addition to waves of ads raising concerns with voters about the measure.

Many of the ads produced by the "No" side made contested claims about the scope of the proposed tax, warning ordinary voters that they could be targeted. Several referenced Newsom's opposition, with a person in one ad noting, "Gavin Newsom, teachers, and firefighters are all voting no. So I'm voting no."

"Governor Gavin Newsom said it best. The wealth tax will damage California," said another ad , backed by more than $3 million worth of airtime. "Newsom, Becerra, and Hilton are all voting no," says a third , referencing the unified opposition between the governor and the two candidates running to succeed him.

According to AdImpact data, the spending gap was dramatic — "No" advertisers outspending "Yes" advertisers by about $140.9 million to just $234,000 on TV, digital, and radio.

Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of the measure as part of the group Yes on 40, accused opponents of running a "deeply misleading and corrupt campaign" and criticized the amount of money they poured into it.

"Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate," Jimenez said in a statement , adding, "The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one. This fight to save patient lives and ensure billionaires pay their fair share has only just begun."

articles.title: Rachel Maddow welcomes 'big fight' between socialist and moderate Democrats after midterm wins
articles.summary: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow told "The View" she hopes moderate Democrats and democratic socialists have a "big fight" that strengthens the party's big tent.
articles.body:
MS NOW host Rachel Maddow told ABC's "The View" Wednesday she hopes there will be a "big fight" between moderate and socialist members of the Democratic Party in Congress.

While promoting her new book "Department of Fate," Maddow discussed recent calls from some progressive senators to replace Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., once Democrats take control of the Senate in January.

Those calling for new leadership included Democratic senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.

Though some Democrats have expressed concerns about infighting within the party, Maddow dismissed those concerns and welcomed the idea of moderate Democrats debating socialists.

"I feel like the Democrats have kind of first-world problems right now," Maddow joked. "There was so much talk ahead of the election about, 'Oh there's these handful of democratic socialist-associated candidates. How are the Democrats going to do?'

"Well, the Democrats elected so many people. Yes, they elected a handful of democratic socialists, but also the Blue Dog coalition, which is the conservative Democrats. They have like a dozen new members too."

Maddow argued that the Democratic Party now includes members with a wide range of political views and that debate could strengthen the party.

"I think that it's righteous for them to have a big fight. I hope they don't settle it instantly. I hope they actually do have a debate. I think competition makes us stronger," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Maddow's comments came one day after "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg called out congressional Democrats publicly debating whether to replace Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as party leaders.

"This is my two cents," Goldberg said. "I don't want to hear this from you right now. I want to know what all of you are, all of you Democrats, what are your plans for the first 100 days? I don't care if you've been there forever or just got there. What are your plans?

"We put you in there to clean house, to make sure that the government works the way the people want it to work," she added. "I don't want to hear all this infighting, because then you become the distraction, and then you become no better than the Republicans were. So, just get your stuff together. All of you."

Democratic strategist and pollster Doug Schoen disagreed with Maddow's assessment.

"It's clear the Dems won an overwhelming victory because of moderates, not progressives. The American people are demanding action on the affordability crisis, not intraparty infighting between progressives and moderates," Schoen told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce, lawyer says, ending long marriage
articles.summary: AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce from his wife, Angela, one of his lawyers said Thursday. It comes nearly a w...
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce from his wife, Angela, one of his lawyers said Thursday.

It comes nearly a week after Paxton, a Republican, lost his U.S. Senate race by double digits to Democrat James Talarico in one of the most expensive contests of the midterm elections that saw a wave of victories for Democrats across the country.

Angela Paxton, a state senator, cited allegations of adultery when she sought to end their 38-year-marriage . She filed the divorce after her husband had launched his run for Senate, posting on social media that she was doing so on "biblical grounds."

Jared Julian, a lawyer for Ken Paxton, said the terms would remain private.

"From my observation, however, they share a mutual respect for one another," Julian said. He added that both appeared to be looking forward "to the next chapters of their lives."

An attorney for Angela Paxton did not immediately respond to phone and email messages Thursday. The finalized divorce was first reported by The New York Times.

After Paxton entered the race, some Republicans considered Paxton a potential drain on GOP resources because of legal, ethical and personal questions he has faced for years.

Angela Paxton had stuck by her husband through a decade of legal troubles that included state and federal corruption investigations and a 2023 state impeachment trial that publicly exposed an extramarital affair.

The Senate race that seemed like a longshot for Democrats when the year began became partly a referendum on Paxton's history . Despite beating the long-seated incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, in a primary and gaining President Donald Trump's endorsement, Paxton struggled to find traction in the general election against Talarico.

In October, less than a month before the election, Angela Paxton urged voters to back the Republican ticket but did not mention her estranged husband by name.

"It's not as much about the individual players on the team. It's about getting the whole team across the finish line," she said in a campaign advertisement.

Democrat Nathan Johnson was elected attorney general and will take office in January.

articles.title: Richard Pontes: quem era o piloto morto em acidente em Manaus | G1
articles.standfirst: Filho do secretário de Produção Rural do Amazonas, Richard Carvalho Pontes tinha 23 anos, era ligado ao automobilismo e havia se tornado pai recentemente.
articles.summary: Conheça a trajetória de Richard Pontes, piloto de 23 anos e filho de secretário que morreu em acidente em Manaus após o nascimento de sua primeira filha.
articles.body:
Richard Carvalho Pontes, de 23 anos, morreu em acidente de trânsito — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Piloto e amante do automobilismo no Amazonas. Assim foi descrito o jovem Richard Carvalho Pontes, de 23 anos, por amigos nas redes sociais. O jovem morreu em um acidente de trânsito na noite de quinta-feira (12), na Avenida das Torres, em Manaus .

Filho do secretário de Produção Rural do Amazonas, Ricelli Pontes, Richard participava do meio automobilístico amazonense. Após a morte do jovem, páginas ligadas ao esporte e ao setor de reparos automotivos publicaram mensagens de pesar nas redes sociais.

A página da pista de arrancada Amazonas Dragway lamentou a morte do piloto e o definiu como uma pessoa querida, que deixou um legado de amizade e respeito no automobilismo.

Outra homenagem foi publicada pela página Família Car Premium 92, que destacou a relação de Richard com o automobilismo e lembrou que o jovem havia se tornado pai recentemente.

Segundo a publicação, Richard era “um pai que estava vivendo um dos momentos mais lindos da vida: a chegada de sua pequena filha recém-nascida” .

Nas mensagens de despedida, amigos também lembraram a atuação do jovem nas pistas, além da amizade e do carinho que mantinha com pessoas próximas.

Richard morreu após sofrer um acidente por volta das 23h50 de quinta-feira. Imagens que circulam nas redes sociais mostram o momento em que o veículo conduzido por ele trafega pela Avenida José Lindoso, conhecida como Avenida das Torres, sai da pista e atinge uma placa de sinalização.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, as equipes que atenderam a ocorrência encontraram o veículo em um barranco, a aproximadamente sete metros da calçada, com Richard preso às ferragens e sem sinais vitais.

Uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) foi acionada, e o médico constatou a morte ainda no local.

O corpo do jovem deu entrada no Instituto Médico Legal (IML) por volta de 1h30 desta sexta-feira (13). Segundo o órgão, a causa da morte foi choque hipovolêmico hemorrágico, provocado por hemorragia interna, com hemotórax e ruptura do átrio direito do coração, em decorrência do acidente de trânsito.

Nas redes sociais, o pai de Richard confirmou a morte do filho. O velório teve início durante a manhã em uma funerária localizada no bairro Praça 14, na Zona Sul de Manaus. Às 14h, o cortejo seguiu para o município de Presidente Figueiredo, no interior do Amazonas.

Carro dirigido por filho de secretário do AM ficou destruído após acidente. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

articles.title: Prazos processuais suspensos por falha na Microsoft, decide Fachin | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a OAB, instabilidade comprometeu ferramentas utilizadas em órgãos do Poder Judiciário em todo o país. Contagem de prazos será retomada na segunda (16).
articles.summary: Prazos processuais suspensos em todo o país após decisão de Edson Fachin motivada por falhas no Microsoft 365; medida atende a pedido urgente feito pela OAB.
articles.body:
O presidente do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ), ministro Edson Fachin , determinou nesta sexta-feira (13) a suspensão da contagem dos prazos processuais em todo o país nos dias 12 e 13 de novembro de 2026.

A medida, que vale também para processos no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), atende a uma solicitação apresentada pelo Conselho Federal da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (OAB) após o registro de falhas graves e instabilidade generalizada nos serviços da Microsoft , iniciadas na última quinta-feira (12).

De acordo com a solicitação, a instabilidade afetou os serviços do Microsoft 365, comprometendo diretamente ferramentas essenciais de comunicação e de trabalho utilizadas pelos órgãos do Poder Judiciário em todo o país.

🗓️ Com a decisão, a retomada oficial da contagem dos prazos processuais ocorrerá na próxima segunda-feira, 16 de novembro de 2026.

A portaria assinada por Fachin também estabelece que eventuais situações específicas que fujam do período exato de 12 e 13 de novembro, mas que tenham sido comprovadamente impactadas pelas falhas tecnológicas da Microsoft, poderão ser analisadas individualmente pelos juízes ou relatores, conforme a legislação processual vigente.

A Microsoft já descartou a hipótese de um ataque hacker e pediu desculpas pelo ocorrido. Na manhã desta sexta, anunciou que os serviços estavam sendo restabelecidos. Entre as plataformas afetadas estão a Microsoft Store, a IA Copilot, Teams, OneDrive, Microsoft Account e Azure, serviço de nuvem corporativa.

Presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin. — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF
tags: Conselho Federal da Ordem dos Advogados

articles.title: Toffoli dá 3 dias para campanha de Lula esclarecer inconsistências nas contas apontadas pelo TSE | G1
articles.standfirst: Técnicos do TSE identificaram indícios de subcontratação e necessidade de comprovar a capacidade de fornecedores pagos com dinheiro do fundo eleitoral.
articles.summary: Técnicos do TSE identificaram indícios de subcontratação e necessidade de comprovar a capacidade de fornecedores pagos com dinheiro do fundo eleitoral.
articles.body:
O ministro Dias Toffoli, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), deu prazo de três dias para a campanha à reeleição da chapa Lula-Alckmin apresentar esclarecimentos sobre inconsistências nas contas apontadas pela área técnica da Corte Eleitoral.

Toffoli deu três dias para que a campanha complemente dados e preste esclarecimentos e justificativas.

Os técnicos identificaram que há indícios de subcontratação irregular e que é necessário comprovar a capacidade operacional dos fornecedores pagos com dinheiro do Fundo Eleitoral (FEFC).

A Assessoria de Exame de Contas Eleitorais e Partidárias (Asepa) afirma que também é preciso ter esclarecimentos e apresentação de documentos para o prosseguimento da análise das contas sobre:

passagens aéreas : necessidade de comprovar que as viagens tinham relação com a campanha e justificar as despesas.

viagens suspeitas : passagens com possíveis incompatibilidades de datas, horários ou itinerários.

transporte e deslocamentos : comprovação de ressarcimentos ao erário, incluindo trajetos realizados, cálculos e comprovantes de pagamento, além de esclarecer eventual utilização de veículos e motoristas oficiais.

propaganda eleitoral : identificação e comprovação de despesas de produção e impulsionamento de propaganda cujo impulsionamento pago havia sido declarado irregular em outro processo.

A análise apontou, a partir do cruzamento de dados entre as prestações de contas eleitorais, que a campanha omitiu R$ 1,5 milhão em doações que não foram registradas.

Lula e Geraldo Alckmin em caminhão em ato da vitória na Avenida Paulista — Foto: Abraão Cruz/TV Globo

articles.title: STF: Bolsonaro feriu liberdade de imprensa ao bloquear perfis no X | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministra, contudo, encerrou ação contra Bolsonaro, afirmando que não cabe mais intervenção da Justiça porque ele deixou o poder e o perfil na plataforma não tem relação com cargo.
articles.summary: Cármen Lúcia afirmou que Bolsonaro violou a liberdade de imprensa ao bloquear jornalistas no X, mas encerrou a ação por ele não ocupar mais a presidência.
articles.body:
A ministra Cármen Lúcia , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), afirmou, em decisão desta sexta-feira (13), que o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro feriu a garantia constitucional da liberdade de imprensa e ofendeu o direito de informação ao bloquear jornalistas na rede social X durante seu mandato.

🔎Ela deu a declaração ao analisar uma ação da Associação Brasileira de Jornalismo Investigativo (Abraji), que foi encerrada por Cármen, uma vez que Bolsonaro não é mais presidente.

Segundo a ministra, as plataformas possuem destaque no debate público e político, especialmente para a circulação de ideias. Cármen Lúcia ressaltou que o perfil do ex-presidente era público e tratava de atos e assuntos governamentais .

Na avaliação da ministra, um governante não pode excluir um cidadão do debate público por questões ideológicas e políticas e isso se torna mais grave se o bloqueio envolve jornalistas, que atuam na fiscalização do poder público .

"A exclusão de alguém da ágora virtual a que se apresentou o então presidente da República em assuntos governamentais e, portanto, políticos, da polis, que é de todos, significa eliminar o cidadão das manifestações públicas de alguém que se comprometeu a desempenhar a função de representante do cidadão que se pretende eliminar daquele espaço público", afirmou Cármen Lúcia.

"Representante não pode se esconder do representado, menos ainda, numa República, excluindo da ágora virtual republicana quem não seja do seu agrado ou interesse. Ninguém é governante de uma República de si mesmo. Por gosto ou desgosto ideológico ou político, não se afasta do debate público o cidadão", completou a ministra.

Cármen Lúcia disse ainda que a responsabilidade decorrente do cargo de presidente da República não permite o afastamento dos atos postados e publicados na condição de representante de "todos os brasileiros" .

"Ao excluir um cidadão do X e selecionar, assim, os cidadãos aos quais permitiu a atividade política de ter ciência de seus atos, opiniões e práticas e negar a manifestação legítima do excluído, optou a autoridade por dirigir-se, por meio de ferramenta de comunicação de alcance público, a apenas a grupos ou pessoas que lhe sejam favoráveis, contrariamente ao princípio constitucional da República e da Democracia", afimrou.

A magistrada apontou que a "situação torna-se ainda mais grave quando as contas bloqueadas por autoridade pública são de jornalistas".

A ação da Abraji foi apresentada em julho de 2021 ao Supremo. A entidade alegou que Bolsonaro teria bloqueado, naquela época, ao menos 65 jornalistas no X. A defesa de Bolsonaro se manifestou e negou a existência de ato ilegal ou abusivo.

Cármen Lúcia ressaltou que um pedido semelhante ao da Abraji, feito por um influenciador, começou a ser analisado em novembro de 2020 pelo plenário virtual do Supremo, mas o ministro Nunes Marques pediu que o caso fosse levado para análise do plenário presencial. E que só em maio deste ano o ministro cancelou o pedido.

Na decisão, a ministra afirmou que não cabe mais a atuação do Supremo porque Bolsonaro deixou a Presidência.

"Desde janeiro de 2023, Jair Bolsonaro não é presidente, portanto, essa condição não mais pode ser considerada para os fins desta impetração, especialmente considerando o caráter particular do perfil com o qual praticou o ato apontado coator", disse.

"O bloqueio dos jornalistas não foi realizado por conta oficial vinculada à Presidência da República, mas por perfil de pessoa que, entre 2019 e 2022, ocupou o cargo de chefe do Poder Executivo da União", acrescentou.

Condenado a 27 anos e três meses de prisão na chamada trama golpista , Bolsonaro atualmente cumpre pena em regime domiciliar e está proibido de usar redes sociais.

Bolsonaro durante entrevista a jornalistas em 2025 — Foto: Evaristo Sá/AFP

articles.title: Mulher negra no STF: Fachin defende indicação para vaga aberta | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do Supremo disse, em encontro de magistrados no Rio, que há juízas negras ‘à altura’ do cargo. A vaga aberta com a aposentadoria de Luís Roberto Barroso segue desocupada.
articles.summary: O presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, afirmou que há magistradas negras capacitadas para ocupar a cadeira deixada por Luís Roberto Barroso na Suprema Corte brasileira.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin , foi aplaudido ao defender, nesta sexta-feira (13), no Rio de Janeiro , a indicação de uma mulher negra para a Corte. A declaração foi feita no encerramento do 9º Encontro Nacional de Juízas e Juízes Negros (Enajun).

"Eu olhava o auditório e eu via as manifestações das magistradas que me precederam e certamente me vinha à cabeça que quem dê direito para definir uma próxima vaga da Suprema Corte Brasileira aqui estivesse saberia que há magistradas negras à altura desse lugar para honrar o Brasil e o povo brasileiro", disse, sendo ovacioado.

A referência foi ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ), a quem cabe indicar um nome para o Supremo. A escolha precisa ser aprovada por pelo menos 41 dos 81 senadores.

O STF nunca teve uma ministra negra. Cármen Lúcia é a única mulher entre os dez integrantes atuais do tribunal.

A cadeira está vaga desde a aposentadoria antecipada de Luís Roberto Barroso , em outubro de 2025. Lula indicou o advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias , mas o Senado rejeitou o nome em abril deste ano, por 42 votos a 34. Foi a primeira vez em 132 anos que o Senado derrubou uma indicação para o Supremo.

O encontro em que Fachin discursou reuniu magistrados para discutir formas de ampliar a presença de pessoas negras nos espaços de decisão do Judiciário. A programação começou na quarta-feira (11) e terminou nesta sexta no Centro Cultural da Justiça Federal, no Centro do Rio.

articles.title: PGR indica que manterá pedido de R$ 324 milhões extras para bancar penduricalhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Manifestação ocorre após a Justiça Federal desistir de pedido de crédito adicional de R$ 208,9 milhões; PGR concorda com pedido da AGU para que STF esclareça regras para abertura de crédito extraordinário.
articles.summary: Manifestação ocorre após a Justiça Federal desistir de pedido de crédito adicional de R$ 208,9 milhões; PGR concorda com pedido da AGU para que STF esclareça regras para abertura de crédito extraordinário.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) indicou nesta sexta-feira (13) que vai manter o pedido de um crédito adicional de R$ 324 milhões para despesas do Ministério Público da União.

O procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, informou ao Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) que "concorda" com o pedido da Advocacia Geral da União para que a Corte esclareça se a Justiça precisa autorizar a abertura de crédito extraordinário para o pagamento das despesas decorrentes do julgamento que definiu novos critérios para o pagamento dos chamados penduricalhos.

🔎 A expressão "penduricalho" é utilizada para se referir a verbas indenizatórias, gratificações e auxílios que são somados ao salário de servidores públicos. Essas gratificações servem para compensar gastos relacionados ao exercício da função ou ressarcir direitos não usufruídos.

A PGR se manifestou a pedido de um dos relatores das ações, o ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Além da Procuradoria, o Conselho da Justiça Federal (CFJ) chegou a pedir um adicional de R$ 208,9 milhões , mas após a repercussão, recuou e disse que novas receitas e ajustes no orçamento eliminaram a necessidade de verba adicional .

Após a mudança de posição do CJF, a AGU afirmou ao Supremo que mantinha o pedido referente ao MPU e que o tribunal poderia esclarecer o modo de cumprimento do julgamento e as providências orçamentárias necessárias à execução das obrigações impostas, considerada a insuficiência de recursos informada pelo MPU .

"À luz dessas razões, considerando o esgotamento da margem disponível no limite individualizado de despesas primárias do MPU, a superveniência de obrigações não contempladas na programação orçamentária de 2026 e a impossibilidade de absorvê-las sem comprometer o funcionamento da instituição, permanece necessária a definição, por essa Suprema Corte, do modo de cumprimento do julgado", afirmou a AGU.

O impasse envolve principalmente a Parcela de Valorização por Tempo de Antiguidade na Carreira (PVTAC), benefício reconhecido pelo STF para integrantes da magistratura e do Ministério Público, autorizada pelo STF em março no julgamento dos penduricalhos .

💰A parcela corresponde a 5% do subsídio a cada cinco anos de efetivo exercício em atividade jurídica, limitada a 35%.

O STF estabeleceu que a PVTAC poderia compor a remuneração de magistrados e membros do Ministério Público enquanto não fosse editada a lei nacional prevista na Constituição para disciplinar as verbas indenizatórias.

Posteriormente, ao analisar recursos apresentados pela PGR, o STF determinou a implantação imediata da parcela, inclusive para inativos e pensionistas, sem a necessidade de requerimento dos interessados.

O Supremo também autorizou a possibilidade de pagamento de outras parcelas , entre elas indenizações por férias e licenças-prêmio não usufruídas por interesse público e auxílio-saúde mediante reembolso, observados os limites estabelecidos na decisão.

articles.title: Vance, Rubio top 2028 list for Republicans, Ossoff and Buttigieg get nod in polling of Democrats
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance lead a new survey of Republican voters on whom they view as a strong presidential candidate in 2028. With the midterms in the rearview, both parties are already beginning to look to the next presidential election. In a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 45 percent of Republican voters…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance lead a new survey of Republican voters on whom they view as a strong presidential candidate in 2028.

With the midterms in the rearview, both parties are already beginning to look to the next presidential election.

In a new Reuters/Ipsos poll , 45 percent of Republican voters said Rubio would make an excellent candidate for president, with another 23 percent saying he would be a good candidate. Only 5 percent said he would be a poor choice.

The vice president was not far behind, with 43 percent rating him an excellent candidate, and another 28 percent rating him as good. Vance has long been considered the front-runner, and recent actions suggest he may be trying to distance himself from unpopular positions of the administration. After the midterms, he was quick to blame the Iran war for GOP losses.

In third place was Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, with a combined 60 percent saying he would be excellent or good, but a sharp drop off emerges after that.

President Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr. is in fourth place, but views of him are very polarized — 38 percent rated him as a poor candidate, more than the combined share of those who said he would be excellent or good. The president’s approval rating in the Reuters/Ipsos poll held steady at a near-record low 32 percent, which may hurt his son’s perception among Republicans.

On the Democratic side, the nomination appears to be wide open, as several candidates have moderate levels of support. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff led the pack, each with 29 percent of Democratic voters saying they would be an excellent candidate. Another 27 percent said Buttigieg would be good, and 20 percent said the same of Ossoff.

Buttigieg, a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., ran in 2020 and performed unexpectedly well, narrowly winning the Iowa caucuses . Ossoff is seen as a top contender after winning reelection in battleground Georgia by nearly 20 points.

Still, more than a third of Democratic voters said they have not heard of him or skipped rating him. More than 20 percent said the same of Buttigieg.

In third place was a candidate nearly all voters had heard of but had polarized views on: 23 percent said former Vice President Kamala Harris would make an excellent candidate, and another 30 percent said she would be a good one. But a combined 45 percent said she would be fair or poor, the most of any candidate surveyed on the Democratic side.

Many of the top candidates on the Democratic side would likely classify themselves as moderates, and the only progressive on the list was Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), with 15 percent saying she would make an excellent candidate, and another 33 percent saying she would be good.

None of the major candidates have yet announced bids for president; but historically, candidates have announced in the weeks and months after the midterm elections. In 2022, President Trump announced his comeback bid just one week after the midterms.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 6-9 among 477 registered Republican voters and 538 registered Democratic voters. The margin of error is 5 points.

articles.title: Alito says Supreme Court is caught between the president and a Congress that can ‘turn off the lights’
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito expressed concern about Congress’ potential use of the power of the purse against the high court in remarks at an event in Washington, D.C., Thursday night.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito expressed concern about Congress’ potential use of the power of the purse against the high court in remarks at an event in Washington, D.C., Thursday night. Speaking with conservative author Mollie Hemingway at a black-tie dinner for the annual Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention, Alito said the judiciary is the “least dangerous” branch of the government, and is “vulnerable to the executive and to Congress because they are more powerful.” “Congress can turn off the lights of the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they will not fund their activities,” he said. “And there are many, many, many other things that they can do, or at least try to do. So it is important to preserve the independence of the judiciary.” Alito did not directly refer to the recent midterm elections, but the conservative stalwart’s remarks came shortly after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in larger than expected numbers last week. Despite the power dynamic, Alito said, that’s “not to say that the federal judiciary cannot be dangerous when it goes to strike.” He referred to the court not as a “nuclear weapon” or a “500-pound bomb,” but a “hand grenade.” “The hand grenade is the least dangerous, but that is not to say that is not dangerous,” Alito said. While stressing the need for judicial independence in remarks to the audience of more than 2,500 conservative elected officials, lawyers, judges, and advocates, Alito also said he believes some federal judges have gone “far astray” in what he called recent “unjustified orders.” That has helped lead, in part, to the rise of the controversial emergency docket over the past 10 or 15 years, said Alito, a nominee of George W. Bush. The Trump administration has had a very high success rate with the conservative majority on the so-called “shadow docket,” with interim rulings that have allowed the administration to move forward with immigration enforcement, the restructuring of the federal government and construction of a White House ballroom while underlying litigation is pending. “Presidents have become very frustrated with their inability to get Congress to enact their legislative agenda, and so they have looked for ways to do as much as they can unilaterally with their own powers,” leading opponents to rush to court to try to block those orders, Alito said. “The litigators, understandably, choose the districts where they think they are most likely to get the result they want. Their expectations are very often met,” he said, and “in some instances,” judges have issued “very sweeping and unjustified orders, stopping what the president wants during during the pendency of appeal,” a process that can take years. “So, if at the end of that period it turns out that the district judge was wrong, the president, whoever it is, will have been prevented for most of a four-year term from implementing this, this, this initiative,” he said. The lower court judges, he said, “are dedicated and they are skillful, but they’re not perfect, and they make mistakes. And in some instances, I think they have gone far astray.”

articles.title: Chris Van Hollen floats using government shutdown threat to force Trump to end Iran war
articles.summary: Chris Van Hollen floated using a government shutdown to pressure President Trump into ending the war in Iran as he challenges Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader.
articles.body: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., floated using a government shutdown to get President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran during an interview on Thursday, after announcing he would challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the incoming Majority Leader position. Van Hollen was asked multiple times during an MS NOW interview how he would be different from Schumer as leader. The senator pointed to ending the war in Iran. "Well, the difference is, I believe we need to be firm," he said. "I think that we heard loud and clear from the American people that they want to end the war in Iran and bring down prices. We shouldn't say we're going to wait until January when we have the power to do it on Dec. 11. And so, this should not be a finger in the wind issue. This should not be sort of frittering around. This should not be a question of timidity. We need to answer the call of the American people, end the war, bring down prices, do it now. Not a penny, not a penny to fuel this war." Congress will need to fund the government by Dec. 11 to avoid a shutdown. MS NOW's Jen Psaki asked Van Hollen if Trump would be "forced" to end the war because Congress couldn't do it unilaterally. FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR "The president would be given a choice, right? Does he say to the American people that 'I'm going to shut down the United States government? Am I going to shut down all the agencies of the U.S. government to keep the illegal war in Iran going and to keep prices high,' when we could do it now?" Van Hollen said. He said Trump could choose to "completely ignore" the will of the American people and shut down the government. Schumer's office did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. The White House also did not return a request for comment. SEN BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS CHRIS VAN HOLLEN'S BID TO CHALLENGE SCHUMER FOR SENATE DEMOCRATIC LEADER POST Van Hollen announced Thursday he would challenge Schumer for the Majority Leader position after Democrats won back the chamber in the 2026 midterms. "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement. "They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people." SCHUMER'S GRIP ON POWER SLIPS AS DEMS BEGIN TO REVOLT AGAINST HIM, EYE NEW LEADERSHIP "It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," he continued. "This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader." Van Hollen, 67, has served in Congress for 23 years, beginning his career in the House before moving to the Senate in 2017. Schumer, 75, has been in Congress since 1981. Liz Mair, a Republican strategist and head of Mair Strategies, told Fox News Digital in a statement, that the shutdown position could be an "effective strategy" for the Democrats. "If you do want to force the Pentagon's hand, this is the easiest way to do it, legislatively, right?" she said. "I think the question is how much reputational downside is there for Democrats?" "Progressives seem to put in quite a lot of confidence in Chris Van Hollen as a prospective leader. And I just wonder whether that's wise on their part," she added, questioning if Van Hollen could execute it. Van Hollen's decision to challenge Schumer comes as several members of the Senate have said they won't support the latter. Longtime allies such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and newer members such as Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., declared this week that they would not back Schumer for leader. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Several senators-elect who rode the blue wave to Washington, D.C., have publicly said they will not support Schumer for leader. Senators-elect Adam Hamilton, Kan., Peggy Flanagan, and Abdul El-Sayed have all publicly rejected the longtime New York senator as the Democratic leader. Van Hollen said he would prioritize restoring Medicaid funding, extending the Affordable Care Act's tax credits, and restoring food and nutrition programs when asked about what he would do in his first 100 days as leader. articles.title: Schumer's former ally mounts leadership challenge as Democrats face rare internal power struggle
articles.summary: Senate Democrats face their first contested leadership race since 1994 as Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer with Bernie Sanders' backing.
articles.body: Senate Democrats are getting an opportunity they haven’t had in decades: a different option for who their leader could be. Even before the blue wave crashed over Republicans and Democrats emerged with a commanding majority in the Senate, the rumblings for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to step aside were there. Now, he’s got a challenger in Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., a familiar face in Washington, D.C., who framed his bid against Schumer as one answering the call for change voters demanded. It’ll be the first time that a Senate Democratic leadership race will be contested since 1994. DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES Van Hollen’s emergence, at 67, as the lone challenger to Schumer, 75, comes after lawmakers and candidates demanded a change in Democratic leadership before the election. That call has only intensified in the week after Democrats won the midterms, with Van Hollen interpreting the seismic political shift as an indictment of President Donald Trump that can only be acted on if Senate Democrats go in a new direction. The challenge is already dividing Senate Democrats. In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen didn’t offer a sharp policy contrast to Schumer, and cast doubt on Democrats’ ability to pass key progressive desires, like Medicare for All. "But it should be very clear: While, you know, voters have rejected the Trump policies, they’ve not yet hired Democrats — they’ve given us a chance, we have to earn their trust," Van Hollen said. "My view is that you can’t earn that trust with old leadership. You need to move on to new leadership." Van Hollen acknowledged that he was an "underdog," but revealed during the interview that he had over 10 Senate Democrats in his corner and believed more were to come. Right now, either lawmaker will need 28 secret ballot votes to win the job — that could bump up to 29 if Democrats flip Alaska, where ballots are still being counted in the Senate race between Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. And it could get messy over the next few weeks before the early December, closed-door election. And he’s got the backing of the progressive standard-bearer in the Senate: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and new faces of the progressive movement, like Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who Van Hollen endorsed early on in his campaign, and Peggy Flanagan, who said on X that Van Hollen was the "leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind." VAN HOLLEN CHALLENGES SCHUMER FOR SENATE LEADERSHIP AFTER DEMOCRATIC ELECTION SWEEP Ultimately, either candidate's success will likely break down on how well they both work with and push back against President Donald Trump. Early in Trump’s second term, Van Hollen won praise from progressives when he traveled to El Salvador for a welfare check on Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident who was mistakenly deported by the administration. But Schumer has dealt with Trump for years, and told the Washington Sun that his strategy heading into the new Congress will be to put bill after bill on the floor, like restoring Obamacare subsidies or banning insider trading, and dare Republicans to vote them down — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., used a similar strategy over the last two years. "In a certain sense, it’s a win-win. I’d rather get things done, but it’s not going to stop us," Schumer said. "We are going to move forward with or without Trump, with or without the Republicans." Despite the demands for change, Van Hollen is very much a creature of Washington, having served in Congress since 2003. He’s the son of diplomats, and served in House Democratic leadership under former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. He was chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the House Democrats’ campaign arm, for two cycles, and was quickly tapped by Schumer to lead the Senate’s campaign operation when he ascended to the upper chamber in 2017. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' And he spent his entire career in the Senate behind Schumer, who first became leader in 2017, and he has rarely broken with him on key votes. He has, however, emerged as a staunch critic of Israel and criticized Schumer’s ties to the crypto industry and meddling in Democratic primaries. He currently serves on four committees in the Senate: Appropriations, Foreign Relations, Budget and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs, and throughout his career in Congress has focused on budget issues and foreign affairs. Still, outside progressive groups are beginning to back him. The progressive Sunrise Movement is all in on Van Hollen. The organization announced its support for the lawmaker on Bluesky, and wrote, "Young people voted for change on election night." "Chuck Schumer can’t give us that, but Chris Van Hollen might," they said. "The truth is, the ‘blue tsunami’ could easily become the blue mirage in the wrong hands. And Schumer’s hands are too full of billionaires’ money to hold young people’s future." Another progressive group, the 50501 protest movement, also declared its support for Van Hollen Thursday night in a post on Bluesky, urging voters to pressure their senators to "vote Chris, NOT CHUCK." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There are a bevy of other outside groups that have opposed Schumer, including Indivisible, MoveOn and the Working Families Party, and the 600,000-member International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers sent the top Democrat a letter demanding he step aside. But Schumer has remained confident about retaining his position. "I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," Schumer said on X. "I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader." His allies have leaned into sports metaphors to describe why he should keep the job, with both Sens. Angus King, I-Maine, and Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., comparing it to a successful manager in baseball. "When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract," Gallego said.Fox News Digital reached out for comment from both Schumer and Van Hollen.

articles.title: Supreme Court to rule on Trump’s asylum ban
articles.summary: The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether President Donald Trump’s administration has the authority to ban asylum claims at the southern border.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Taking up another key aspect of President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration agenda, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the administration has the authority to ban asylum claims at the southern border. Although a federal judge ruled that the policy Trump enacted on the first day of his second term was unlawful, it has remained in effect while litigation continues. The Supreme Court’s ruling, due before the end of June, will be the final word on the Trump administration’s sweeping assertion of presidential power over people trying to make asylum claims at the border, notwithstanding federal law enacted by Congress that lays out a procedure to do so. The asylum dispute is the third significant case on Trump’s immigration policies that the court is considering, while the justices could take up other Trump-related cases in the coming months. The ban stems from a proclamation the president issued Jan. 20, 2025, that declared an “invasion” on the southern border. Under one of its provisions, anyone who crosses the border without required paperwork can immediately be removed without the ability to claim asylum. Immigration hawks have long complained that people who enter the country illegally apply for asylum in order to stay in the country while their cases are processed, even if they do not have valid claims. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in court papers that the president has sweeping authority to bar entry to the U.S., both under specific federal immigration laws and the powers delegated to him in the Constitution. The policy “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens,” Sauer wrote. He pointed to a provision of immigration law that says the president can restrict entry of anyone when he deems it would be “detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The policy was challenged by 13 unnamed plaintiffs, as well as three immigration groups: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project. Their lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union argue that the ban flouts the asylum rules implemented by Congress in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). Under that process, immigrants can argue that they have “credible fear” of torture or persecution if they are returned to their home country. The president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute,” they wrote in court papers. In July 2025, Washington-based U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss ruled against the administration, saying that nothing in the Constitution or immigration law “grants the president ... authority to replace the comprehensive rules and procedures set forth in the INA.” In April this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld Moss’ ruling, leading the administration to seek Supreme Court review. In one of the two other immigration cases on the Supreme Court docket, the justices will consider the administration’s ongoing efforts to deport immigrants to “third countries” they have no previous connection to if they cannot be returned to their home nations. The other case concerns the administration’s attempt to detain indefinitely thousands of people in deportation proceedings, a break from previous administrations, which released those immigrants while their cases were adjudicated. The asylum case follows a related ruling in favor of the president’s authority over the border in June. The Supreme Court has had a steady stream of Trump-related immigration cases dating back to his first term, when it upheld his travel ban on people from mostly Muslim-majority countries entering the United States. But in June, the court delivered a major blow to Trump when it blocked his executive order seeking to limit the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship.

articles.title: Supreme Court will decide if Trump’s asylum restrictions are legal
articles.summary: The Supreme Court announced Friday it will hear the Trump administration’s case to revive the president’s asylum restrictions at the southern border, issued on Inauguration Day and since ruled illegal by lower courts. The case, set to be heard this term with a decision expected by summer, will mark one of the court’s highest-profile confrontations…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court announced Friday it will hear the Trump administration’s case to revive the president’s asylum restrictions at the southern border, issued on Inauguration Day and since ruled illegal by lower courts.

The case, set to be heard this term with a decision expected by summer, will mark one of the court’s highest-profile confrontations with President Trump’s second-term immigration crackdown.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the policy Trump’s “main tool” for stopping illegal crossings. Lower courts invalidated it, though the policy has remained in effect as the appeal proceeds.

“And as several high-ranking government officials have explained, if allowed to take effect, the order below threatens to open the floodgates to illegal entry, once again overwhelming the system and rendering the southern border vulnerable to the trafficking of drugs, weapons, and other contraband and enabling cartels to re-establish control,” Sauer wrote in court filings.

Trump signed the proclamation on his first day back in office. It declared an “invasion” at the southern border and categorically predenied the filing of asylum applications.

Asylum — a pathway for those fleeing persecution and danger to seek refuge in the U.S. — has become an increasingly common claim by those crossing between ports of entry.

Asylum seekers, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and immigration groups, quickly sued over Trump’s proclamation, saying that illegal crossing was already in decline and the policy eviscerates noncitizens’ legal rights at the border.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss, an appointee of former President Obama, agreed Trump’s policy exceeded his authority and blocked it . The administration brought the case to the Supreme Court after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the judge’s ruling in April.

GOP voices have argued that asylum has been abused by many migrants, including those coming to the U.S. for economic opportunities rather than to escape violence.

The protections are only granted to those being persecuted for political views or other characteristics like religious beliefs or their sexuality.

But those who pass an initial screening are allowed into the country to pursue the claim in immigration court, where a yearslong backlog means migrants are often able to spend significant time within the U.S. before their case is heard.

The asylum battle is one of two new cases the Supreme Court took up Friday. The justices also said they’d hear Robinhood’s appeal in an investor lawsuit concerning its disclosures as the company went public.

articles.body:
Democrat Eileen Laubacher is projected to win Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Laubacher defeated incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), unseating one of President Trump’s most outspoken allies in a district that has long favored the GOP. DDHQ rated the seat “likely Republican” heading into Election Day.

The Democrat notched 48.8 percent of the vote, while the incumbent garnered 47.8 percent, with more than 95 percent of the vote tallied as of Friday.

The victory cuts short Boebert’s congressional career after six years on Capitol Hill, including a controversial district switch that helped her secure a third term in 2024.

The Colorado Republican first arrived in Washington in 2021 after winning the state’s 3rd District, quickly establishing herself as a prominent figure in the House GOP’s conservative wing. But her political fortunes became increasingly uncertain in 2022, when she narrowly survived a challenge from Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes.

Rather than face another potentially difficult reelection fight, Boebert announced in late 2023 that she would run in the 4th District, which was being vacated by retiring GOP Rep. Ken Buck.

The move paid off, and she won the seat in 2024 by roughly 12 percentage points, securing another two years in Congress.

This time, however, she faced a well-funded challenge from Laubacher, a retired two-star Navy admiral and former GOP member who made her military background and national security experience central to her campaign.

The Democrat spent 34 years in the Navy, including assignments in Afghanistan and India, and later served on the National Security Council in former President Biden’s administration. She also built a significant fundraising advantage, bringing in millions more than Boebert during the campaign, Federal Election Commission filings show .

Laubacher emphasized affordability, healthcare and fiscal responsibility, while criticizing Trump’s tariffs and the administration’s handling of the war with Iran.

Boebert, meanwhile, leaned into her support for Trump’s agenda, particularly on immigration and border security.

articles.title: Two top Trump Cabinet officials go to war over China spy scandal amid explosive accusations: report
articles.summary: A White House Situation Room meeting erupted after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy tied to chip diversions was revealed.
articles.body: A White House Situation Room meeting reportedly turned into a blowout between two of President Donald Trump's Cabinet secretaries after news broke that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspect Chinese spy. Tempers apparently boiled over regarding claims Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick dragged his feet on placing restrictions on a company run by a suspected Chinese spy with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, even after the Cabinet official received an intel memo informing him of the potential threat. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly confronted Lutnick about that in the meeting, and other Cabinet officials took Bessent's side, according to Axios. Trump has for months called to place companies suspected of supplying China with Nvidia's complex AI chips on what is called the Entity List, a Department of Commerce export control list that identifies companies the U.S. government believes pose a serious risk to national security. A SPY TOOK OUT NVIDIA’S CEO; HERE’S HOW AMERICA STILL WINS THE AI RACE Three times — in May, August and last Thursday — Trump approved taking action against companies believed to be diverting Nvidia chips to China, according to Axios. One of those companies is Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is reportedly one of Nvidia's largest customers. Suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, with whom the former Nvidia CEO admitted to having an affair, is an executive at Megaspeed. Lutnick was accused of slow-rolling in putting Megaspeed on the Entity List, which prompted Bessent to lose his patience. When the news of Jensen Huang's affair broke, Lutnick, Bessent, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reportedly convened in the Situation Room. Bessent confronted Lutnick about why the export controls had not already been put into place, and others in the room took Bessent's side, according to the Axios report. REBECCA GRANT: JENSEN HUANG OWES AMERICA AN APOLOGY, AND NVIDIA OWES INVESTORS ANSWERS Lutnick said he would have to discuss it with the president despite Trump's May and August orders to proceed. The group then met with Trump later in the day at the Oval Office. The president reportedly gave the order again, saying, "Let's get it done." Still, Lutnick wouldn't proceed. "I'll develop some options and come back," he said. The group replied that Trump's decision was final and that Lutnick must "go f---ing execute." Lutnick is at the center of the scandal, especially after it was revealed he received a memo informing him about U.S. intelligence that Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and still did nothing to put the company she ran on the Entity List. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS A spokesperson for the Commerce Department didn't directly address the report of Lutnick's confrontation with Bessent. "The Department of Commerce and the Department of the Treasury have a great working relationship and are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda," Kristen Eichamer told Fox News. She also said Lutnick has proactively decided to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions on the matter. A hearing is scheduled for Dec. 10. Bessent appeared on CNBC's "Sqwuak Box" Thursday morning, where he was asked about the reported blowout. He said there was coordination between the various agencies about putting Megaspeed on the Entity List but then referred further questions to the Commerce Department and Bureau of Industry and Security. "You will have to ask them about their internal proceedings," Bessent said. articles.title: Rep. Lauren Boebert, conservative firebrand from Colorado, loses her race for re-election
articles.summary: The Colorado Republican changed to a more conservative district after a close re-election call in 2022. But this year’s blue tsunami has swept her out of office, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., a conservative firebrand who was caught up in several headline-grabbing controversies during her six years in Congress, has been defeated by Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, NBC News projects. Laubacher is a retired Navy rear admiral and Afghanistan war veteran who served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration. “Integrity matters. Character matters. Truth matters, and public service should always be about what you can do for other people, not what you do for yourself,” Laubacher told supporters on election night, according to The Colorado Sun. “Those things were worth fighting for when we started.” Boebert, who won re-election in Colorado’s 3rd District by just 546 votes in 2022, shifted to the much redder 4th Congressional District in 2024 and won re-election more easily. But that shift proved no match for the anti-Trump blue tsunami that washed over the country in these midterm elections, sweeping her and many other GOP incumbents out of office. “There was a lot of money dumped on my head,” Boebert said after the election, while also blaming the Senate for failing to pass many House-approved Republican bills. Before her political career, Boebert was a gun-rights activist and owned Shooters Grill in Rifle, Colorado. She upset Rep. Scott Tipton, R-Colo., in the GOP primary in 2020 and became a vocal defender of Donald Trump in Washington. But their relationship soured more recently. In November 2025, Boebert was one of four Republicans who joined Democrats in signing a discharge petition to force a vote to release the Justice Department’s Jeffrey Epstein files, against Trump’s will. When Trump vowed to unseat Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., for leading the Epstein files push, Boebert sided with Massie and campaigned with him this May. Trump lashed out, calling her “dumb” and “weak-minded,” and threatened to rescind his endorsement of her, though he never did. Boebert was known on Capitol Hill more for her controversies and clashes with fellow lawmakers than for legislative savvy. In 2021, she apologized after video emerged of her suggesting that fellow Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was mistaken for a terrorist in an elevator both were riding in the Capitol. Omar said Boebert’s description of the two riding an elevator never happened. At the State of the Union address in 2022, Boebert and then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., stood up and heckled President Joe Biden throughout his speech, including trying to start a “build the wall” chant. The two conservative women later had a very public falling-out, with Greene calling her colleague “a little b----” on the House floor. In 2023, Boebert and her date were escorted out of a performance of the “Beetlejuice” musical in Denver. They were alleged to have been vaping, taking photos and engaging in other disruptive behavior.

articles.title: Lauren Boebert, once a MAGA star, loses her Colorado seat
articles.summary: Boebert, who rose to fame as one of Donald Trump's biggest cheerleaders, will not serve a fourth term in Congress.
articles.body:
Lauren Boebert, the Republican representative from Colorado who rose to national fame as one of Donald Trump's biggest cheerleaders, has lost her seat in Congress.

The race was too close to call on election night last week, but after every vote was counted the Democrat Eileen Laubacher has been declared the winner by the AP news agency.

It means Boebert, who was one of the most vocal conservatives in the House of Representatives, will not serve a fourth term.

The 39-year-old was one of the faces of Trump's "Make America Great Again" - or MAGA - movement, when she burst on to the Colorado political scene at the end of 2019.

Like the president, she was not a career politician. Boebert first made headlines when she encouraged staff at her restaurant Shooters, located in a small Colorado town named Rifle, to openly carry firearms.

Her rallies focused on gun rights and fighting - fighting Democrats, fighting the establishment, fighting illegal immigration or fighting anyone or anything that could be deemed "woke".

"Speaking after Lauren Boebert was like the band that played after the Beatles - no-one remembered them," said Republican state representative Matt Soper, now Colorado's most senior Republican legislator.

He first met Boebert and her then-husband, Jayson, when she was gathering signatures for a state-voting initiative.

She arrived in jeans with a Glock on her hip, her husband "looking like a classic oilman" in blue jeans, boots, cowboy hat and belt buckle, Soper told the BBC.

It played well with her Western Colorado constituency - a mix of ranches, farms and tough terrain with a smattering of ski towns - which Trump won with 53% of the vote in 2016.

Those same voters embraced Boebert in the lead-up to the 2020 election, helping her unseat the five-term Republican incumbent in the party's primary.

Boebert earned her high school equivalency diploma right before that victory, then won the seat in November, just before her 34th birthday.

It was the start of a political career Soper did not anticipate after that first meeting with her and her spouse.

"If I had been told, you know, they're going to make not just national headlines, but international headlines, for years, and Lauren will be a member of Congress for six years, I mean, I would have put no money on that bet," he said.

Once in Congress, Boebert garnered constant airtime with her aggressive pro-Trump rhetoric. Along with fellow political provocateurs like Marjorie Taylor Greene, she established herself as one of the most outspoken MAGA cheerleaders.

Perhaps most notably, she joined Greene in heckling President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address.

But that knack for the limelight began to work against Boebert at home.

"I think, as that national profile grew, it made it much harder for her to be able to maintain that small-town fighter narrative that she had relied on," Justin Gollob, a political science professor at Colorado Mesa University, told the BBC.

Waning enthusiasm for Boebert became glaringly apparent in 2022, when a Democrat from Aspen challenged her for her seat and nearly won. Boebert eked out a victory by just 546 votes.

Colorado voters had initially liked Boebert's "straight talk and her direct, down-the-barrel approach" as well as her conservative Christian views, said Rich Wyatt, a county Republican chairman in Colorado and former reality star who served time in prison for tax fraud.

But that narrative became harder for her to maintain as the congresswomen was beset by controversies that were personal, not political.

She filed for divorce from her husband and, five months later, footage of Boebert and a man being kicked out of a Denver performance of the musical Beetlejuice went viral.

Staff accused the politician of vaping, taking pictures and "causing a disturbance".

Footage released by the theatre showed Boebert, in a gold cocktail dress, arguing with staff before twirling and dancing with her date upon ejection.

An incident report claimed she had told staff "do you know who I am?" and "I will be contacting the mayor," the Denver Post reported.

That December - facing another matchup with Adam Frisch, the former Aspen Democratic councilman who nearly unseated her - Boebert announced she would be switching districts altogether. She moved across the state to Colorado's easternmost constituency, which voted reliably Republican.

With Trump's endorsement, Boebert won the seat in 2024.

But she turned on the president during his second term in office, when she became one of four House Republicans pushing for the full release of the Epstein files.

Suddenly, her biggest champion was no longer in her corner.

The next month, Trump vetoed a water bill Boebert had sponsored. As she sought re-election this year, he took aim at her on social media.

The president invited candidates to run against her in the primary (though the deadline had already passed) and called his former cheerleader "dumb" and "weak-minded".

Trump eventually endorsed Boebert for the race, but Democrats had found a strong moderate candidate to take her on - Navy veteran Eileen Laubacher, who retired in 2024 as a two-star rear admiral.

Like several other Democrats who have emerged victorious after the 2026 midterms, Laubacher's win is as much about her qualities as a candidate - she was a former Republican with strong appeal to middle-ground voters - as it was a rebuke of Boebert's time in office.

Peggy Lozen, a constituent who voted for Trump in 2016 but not after that, was thrilled to see Boebert go. She had been turned off by the representative since her State of the Union stunt in 2022.

"I was sick over that," the 72-year-old told BBC. "I was raised in an era where you respect everyone, regardless of their opinion, and especially the president of the United States."

The mother of a veteran, she voted for the rear admiral and displayed a sign of support in her yard.

"You can't even compare the two," she said of Laubacher and Boebert.

While it remains to be seen what Boebert does next, there is a consensus among both politicians and the public that she is unlikely to vanish altogether.

"I'll leave you with this," Wyatt said: "You haven't seen the end of Lauren Boebert."

articles.title: DeSantis on Defense secretary speculation: ‘I’ve never discussed it’ with Trump
articles.summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said he has “never discussed” replacing Pete Hegseth as Defense secretary with President Trump despite recent speculation. “I see President Trump frequently now that he’s back in Florida, I’ve never discussed it with him. It’s never been anything that I’ve asked,” DeSantis said when asked if he would be…
articles.body:
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said he has “never discussed” replacing Pete Hegseth as Defense secretary with President Trump despite recent speculation.

“I see President Trump frequently now that he’s back in Florida, I’ve never discussed it with him. It’s never been anything that I’ve asked,” DeSantis said when asked if he would be interested in replacing the Defense secretary during a Fox News podcast interview .

The calls for Hegseth’s impeachment came as Democrats secured a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, winning key races in states like Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas. The efforts were spearheaded by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who introduced eight articles of impeachment — accusing the Defense secretary of abusing his powers, including during the war in Iran.

On Tuesday, House Republicans voted to shelve the impeachment measure in a tight 211-204 vote, placing a halt on the effort until the next Congress.

Last week, CBS News reported that DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth’s position, citing one unnamed source. A source, however, said the Florida governor is not interested in the role .

Massie, this week, told reporters that DeSantis would be “great” at the job, adding, “he understands the legality and constitutional boundaries between the legislative and the executive branch, so he’d be great at that. But I’m only telling you his name because I think he probably doesn’t want it.”

“I think you can disagree with a cabinet secretary, but to just try to use impeachment on policy grounds and policy difference, I don’t think that that’s a good precedent,” DeSantis said during the interview.

“I think the Republicans were right to say no to that, and I think the President’s right to stand by his secretary and not cave to that type of tactic,” he added.

The president has stood by Hegseth amid the impeachment calls, reaffirming his support and confidence in him during an interview with CBS News’s 60 Minutes , which aired Sunday. In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, the president gave Hegseth an “A” plus for his work at the Pentagon and called Massie “a TOTAL LOSER.”
