articles.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events ahead of law banning local DEI funding
articles.summary: The city credits the decision to a piece of legislation championed by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.
articles.body:
DELRAY BEACH, Fla. ( WFLA ) — A city in Florida announced this week that it will not host its annual St. Patrick’s Day Parade or Pride event in 2027, crediting the decision to a piece of legislation championed by Gov. Ron DeSantis (R).

DeSantis had signed SB 1134 into law in April, restricting municipal funding, promotion, and official actions involving activities that the law defines as diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) as of Jan. 1, 2027. The restrictions include “programming, or activities designed or implemented with reference to race, color, sex, ethnicity, gender identity, or sexual orientation,” according to the bill.

The City of Delray Beach, in messages posted to Facebook and its St. Patrick’s Day parade website , said it believed the Pride and St. Patrick’s Day parades violate these stipulations.

“Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, or promoting these events in 2027,” a Facebook message posted to the city’s official page reads.

The post shared to the city’s St. Patrick’s Day parade website, meanwhile, says the parade can go on as planned if it’s not funded or planned by the city, but rather private entities or individuals. On his own Facebook page, Carney said the city is now “working feverishly with multiple entities” to put the parade back on.

Carney did not mention whether Delray Beach is also working with sponsors to put on its Pride festivities. But he reportedly said he would support private funding for the Pride parade as well, local outlet CBS12 reported.

In the meantime, Delray Beach officials said the legislation still allows for celebrations of federal holidays (of which St. Patrick’s day is not) and could continue to plan for such events.

“We remain committed to serving all residents and providing opportunities for community engagement consistent with applicable state and federal laws,” the St. Patrick’s Day parade site reads.

DeSantis, responding to a news article on Delray Beach’s decision, claimed on X that the city is engaging in “malicious compliance.”

“What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law. It’s just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We’ve seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat,” DeSantis wrote.

Critics, however, promptly pointed out that Delray Beach’s interpretation of SB 1134’s language appeared to be valid, no matter the reasoning for their choice to obey the law.

“The best way to get rid of a bad rule/law is to follow it,” one X user wrote. “Today’s lesson: Don’t create stupid rule/laws.”

images.caption: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks during a news conference Aug. 12, 2025, in Tampa, Fla. (Chris O’Meara, Associated Press file)

articles.title: Lauren Boebert loses House seat to Democratic challenger in Colorado
articles.summary: The congresswoman had switched districts in the 2024 election to one that favored Republicans, but it wasn't enough to insulate her from widespread Democrati...
articles.body:
In what had been considered Colorado's most Republican-leaning congressional district, incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert has been defeated by Democrat Eileen Laubacher.

The Associated Press called the race on Friday afternoon.

Laubacher received 48.8% of the vote (187,488 votes) to Boebert's 47.9% (184,047 votes), with 99% of the vote counted. Douglas Mangeris, a libertarian, received 3.3%, or 12,720 votes, per AP.

Boebert, an outspoken gun rights activist, has served in Congress since 2021 and is considered one of President Trump's staunchest allies on Capitol Hill.

Laubacher is a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral who was deployed in Afghanistan. She also served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden.

Laubacher's victory adds Colorado's 4th District to the more than 40 Republican-held districts that have flipped to Democrats this midterm cycle, including two others in Colorado.

In an interview with NewsNation on Thursday, Boebert blamed her impending loss on "so many different variables" that plagued Republicans across the country, including gas prices, the war in Iran and Congress's failure to address corruption in the U.S. political system.

She also argued that she and other members of the right wing House Freedom Caucus "weren't heard" when they called for Congress to take action on a variety of issues that voters care about, including government surveillance and "fair elections."

The result is indicative of the remarkable swing toward Democrats that took place in historically safe Republican districts across the country. Boebert, who relocated from Colorado's more-purple 3rd District in 2023, won by more than 11 percentage points the last time she was on the ballot.

Laubacher served 34 years in the U.S. Navy, working in a variety of intelligence and command positions, before retiring in 2024. Her father also spent his career in the Navy, reaching the rank of vice admiral. Her grandfather served as a Navy combat diver during World War II. Laubacher spent significant periods of her Navy career abroad, including a deployment to Afghanistan in 2009 and service in a senior role at the U.S. Embassy in India.

Though she said she had frequently told people in her life that she would "never run for office," Laubacher opted to enter the race for Boebert's seat because she believed residents of Colorado's 4th District deserved "serious and honest representation" in Congress.

Laubacher had reportedly been a Republican throughout much of her life before registering as a Democrat in late 2025. Her decision to switch parties, she said, was driven by her view that the Republican Party had become "nearly unrecognizable" to her.

Laubacher's recent party swap became the subject of a lawsuit during the Democratic primary, with one of the other Democrats in the race attempting to prevent her from qualifying for the ballot. That effort failed, and Laubacher later secured the Democratic nomination.

In terms of policy, Laubacher is firmly within the moderate wing of the Democratic Party. She supports strong immigration enforcement, tax cuts for the middle class and reducing the national debt. She placed a heavy emphasis on affordability throughout her campaign, including calling on President Trump to repeal tariffs that raise consumer prices and end the war with Iran.

First elected to represent Colorado's 3rd District in 2020, Boebert quickly became one of the more vocal and recognizable members of the House Republican caucus. She has been a persistent critic of the "deep state" and was a staunch supporter of Trump's efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

During her first year in the House, she introduced separate resolutions to impeach then-President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris over their handling of the U.S. military withdrawal from Afghanistan. In 2023, she was one of the key voices behind a leadership battle among House Republicans that was only settled when Kevin McCarthy was elected Speaker after 15 roll call votes. Later that year, she mounted a second unsuccessful effort to impeach Biden.

Boebert's personal life drew scrutiny in September 2023 after she and a male companion were escorted out of a stage production of Beetlejuice for allegedly "vaping, singing, [and] causing a disturbance." Though she initially denied acting inappropriately, she later apologized for her behavior, saying that her actions "fell short of my values."

Though Boebert won her first House race by a comfortable margin, she narrowly avoided defeat in her bid for reelection in 2022, defeating her Democratic challenger by just 546 votes. Prior to the 2024 election, Boebert switched her reelection bid to Colorado's 4th District, a region of the state considered "far more favorable to Republicans."

The move proved effective in helping Boebert secure a comfortable victory in 2024. But the redder district was not enough to insulate her from the widespread Democratic gains across the country this year.

images.caption: Lauren Boebert and Eileen Laubacher. (Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images, Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post via Getty Images)

articles.title: Pete Hegseth impeachment effort dies in the House as absent Democrats couldn't beat the traffic
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided becoming only the third cabinet secretary ever impeached after 11 absent Democrats failed to reach the House floor.
articles.body: Most of America bemoans political gridlock in the nation’s capital. DC area commuters deplore the city’s transit gridlock. But Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth may now be a fan of DC’s legendary traffic snarls. It appears that crosstown traffic may have prevented him from becoming only the third Cabinet secretary ever impeached by the House of Representatives. The House voted 211-204 this week to divert an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Hegseth. House Republicans moved to block a straight, up-or-down vote on impeachment. Instead, Republicans forced a vote on sending the articles to the Judiciary Committee. That’s where they’d go to die. If the House failed to sidetrack the articles, Members would have then voted on actual impeachment. If a simple majority voted to impeach, Hegseth would join 19th century Secretary of War William Belknap and former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas as the only Cabinet Members impeached by the House. But DC’s streetside congestion altered the parliamentary traffic on the House floor. All Democrats said they were intent on impeaching Hegseth. But Republicans faced an attendance problem. Seven of their Members were missing. The vote on sending the impeachment articles to committee was tight. The tally read 204-204 at one point. By rule, tie votes fail. That would have compelled a vote on actual impeachment. But a few more Republicans trickled in. The absent Democrats never did. Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) presided over the vote. He gaveled it closed at 211 yeas to send the articles to the committee and 204 votes against. That was it. The Hegseth impeachment quest was dead. Eleven Democrats missed the roll call. It’s about the math. Flip four votes and Hegseth would have been impeached, 208-207. HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS And, had all 11 truant Democrats made it to the U.S. Capitol and voted, it’s likely the House would have impeached Hegseth 215-211. Even eight Democrats would have made it 212-211. However, thanks to the Democrats’ attendance issue, Republicans were able to tap the brakes on the impeachment interstate. The failure to impeach Hegseth is now fueling road rage in the Democratic Party. "Shame on them for not showing up," said Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.). "I don't make excuses for colleagues who don't show up on such an important vote," said Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.). Democrats can’t beat Republicans if they can’t beat the traffic. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) is one of the most outspoken Democrats when it comes to her disdain for Hegseth. But Stansbury grew defensive when questioned by colleague Bill Melugin about missing the vote. "I was trapped right there at that street corner because there was a police motorcade moving busses off of the campus. And I physically was trapped right at that corner in my vehicle, in traffic because the police had shut down traffic," said Stansbury. "Why not come here sooner, though?" followed up Melugin. HEGSETH COULD FACE NEW IMPEACHMENT PUSH OVER UKRAINE AID, LAWMAKERS WARN "I did and I was trapped in my vehicle because of a police motorcade," said Stansbury. Maybe. Maybe not. The Constitution’s "Speech or Debate" clause exempts lawmakers from police interference when "going to and from" the Capitol for "their attendance at the Session of their Respective Houses." It’s kind of like diplomatic immunity. A few years ago, Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) was supposed to preside over a brief House session in the middle of a recess. Traffic heading into DC from Northern Virginia was stopped because of an incident. Beyer was the only Member scheduled to be present in the House chamber that day. So Beyer identified himself to a police officer who proceeded to let him through. Over the years, other lawmakers have asserted the Speech or Debate clause as a reason to bypass unrelated police activity and get to Capitol Hill. Reps. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) and Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.) also said they were stuck in traffic. However, Rep. Lou Correa (D-Calif.) was out for a medical procedure. Rep. Steve Horsford (D-Nev.) missed the vote because of a personal emergency. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) was in the Golden State. DC’s traffic interfered with parliamentary traffic again on Thursday morning. The House took an early Thursday morning vote related to a veterans bill. The House adopted the motion, 271-135. But the House gaveled down the vote with 26 Members absent. The reason? Some Members were again stymied from making it to the Capitol. Emergency room physician Matt Lambert killed one person at a gym, shot six people and engaged in a standoff with cops before turning the gun on himself. Initially reported as an "active shooter" incident, District of Columbia police locked down major parts of the city, stalling traffic. And that’s why some lawmakers missed Thursday’s roll call. They were marooned in traffic. Shifting gears, Rep. Eric Sorensen (D-Ill.) in fact made that procedural vote on the floor. When the vote began, a gentle breeze blew across the Capitol plaza. Then a mist enveloped the Capitol. Later, a few heavier drops. Then the sun broke through the clouds. But reverted to overcast. It was a dank morning in Washington. "I want to know what the weather is," yours truly shouted at Sorensen as he skipped down the House steps toward a group of reporters waiting below. Sorensen is a meteorologist who worked for decades at TV stations in Texas and Illinois before coming to Washington in 2023. Sorensen pivoted immediately into weatherman mode. "We've got increasing showers guys. Much cooler temperatures for the weekend," said Sorensen, replicating the precise forecast for Washington, DC over the next few days. The meteorologist-turned-lawmaker gestured to his right as though looking at a phantom map of the Midwest, projected against a green screen in a TV studio. "As God is my witness, I cannot talk about the weather without moving my hands," said Sorensen. "I talk about high pressure. It's high pressure right here in the midsection of the country. And it's moving in our direction for the next week." After the election, the political weather forecast would seem good for Democrats right now. Supposedly balmy days and comfortable nights. A political "high", if you will. "So is there a high-pressure system moving here for the Democratic Caucus?" yours truly asked. "No. It's low pressure, man. It's low pressure going into the next Congress. We’ve just got to keep everybody together," he replied. But is a high-pressure system really in the long-range forecast for Democrats? Or will a political "low" bring storms and atmospheric volatility — especially if progressive and centrist Democrats tangle with one another? articles.title: House Democrats’ campaign arm investigates sexual harassment allegation against Poindexter

In the interest of fairness to all parties involved, we have hired an independent,…
articles.body:
House Democrats’ campaign arm is investigating Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter (D-Ohio) for an allegation of sexual harassment, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) confirmed to The Hill on Friday.

“The DCCC has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously. In the interest of fairness to all parties involved, we have hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts. Upon completion of that investigation … the DCCC will have further comment,” DCCC executive director Julie Merz said in a statement.

A spokesperson for Poindexter’s campaign said it is aware of the interaction being investigated and that Poindexter thought he made a harmless comment to a volunteer on his campaign, but he later learned how the woman felt.

“Brian gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer. He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful,” the spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill. “When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable.”

Poindexter recently defeated the embattled Rep. Max Miller (R) in the race for Ohio’s 7th District.

Miller was facing allegations of domestic abuse against his ex-wife and young daughter, which he denied. The Ohio Republican’s ex-wife is the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), who at the time the allegations came out said Miller needed “serious psychological help.”

Some Senate Republicans abandoned support for Miller’s reelection bid in solidarity with Moreno. Miller ultimately lost to Poindexter by nearly 10 percentage points in a district President Trump carried by 11 points in 2024.

Poindexter is set to be sworn in with the new Congress on Jan. 3.

Politico previously reported that some key Democratic fundraising groups removed Poindexter from their endorsement lists before the allegation emerged.

articles.summary: Chuck Schumer faces a rare contested Senate leadership race as Chris Van Hollen pushes to abolish the filibuster and shake up Democratic strategy.
articles.body: DENVER — A mile above much of the country, and leagues away from Washington, D.C., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is facing a progressive rebellion that threatens his grip on power. The challenge is being led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has served under Schumer since 2017. And he is willing to go further than Schumer ever has on one issue: terminating the filibuster. Years ago, Schumer tried and failed to narrowly change the Senate’s rule to pass a sweeping voting rights package. Republicans have toyed with it over the last two years, but never pulled the trigger. SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE Van Hollen said, "We need democracy in the United States Senate, and that means allowing, ultimately, a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people. "So, that means 51 votes. So, my personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic … provision. It's not in our Constitution," Van Hollen added. "It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people." Van Hollen announced his challenge against Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, Thursday night after a listening campaign with Senate Democrats. It presents a rare opportunity for Senate Democrats since there hasn’t been a contested Democratic leadership election since 1994. Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump. "I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, where Democratic leaders, strategists and activists gathered to debate the party’s direction after its midterm wins. Van Hollen framed his challenge to Schumer as a response to voters’ calls for change after Democrats’ sweeping wins and President Donald Trump’s policies. "I did discuss this with Senator Schumer," Van Hollen told Fox News Digital. "We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice." Van Hollen has also criticized Schumer for limiting votes on legislation popular with Democrats, including a bill to boost unions. He said the incoming majority should pass the bills candidates campaigned on and challenge Trump to respond. "We shouldn’t wait to hear what President Trump may or may not do," Van Hollen said. "We should answer the call of the American people." Toppling Schumer will be an uphill climb. As the incumbent leader, he has an established network of support and can offer colleagues leadership posts. Either candidate will need 28 votes in the secret ballot contest expected in early December or 29 if Democrats win Alaska, where ballots are still being counted in the Senate race between Democratic nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Ara, also of Denver, was optimistic about Van Hollen’s chances, saying she believes he already has significant support. "I think there’s a really good chance," Ara told Fox News Digital. articles.title: Paraguay’s ex-president Pena faces new charge over Ueno bank collapse
articles.summary: The criminal association charge over his alleged role in the collapse of the bank comes a week after his removal.
articles.body:
Paraguayan prosecutors have charged former president Santiago Pena with criminal association over his alleged role in the collapse of the digital bank Ueno , a week after Congress removed him from office.

The prosecutor’s office announced the new charge on Friday, adding to the breach of trust and self-dealing charges already facing Pena, who is being held in pretrial detention at a military facility.

The 47-year-old former leader is accused of using his position to direct millions in government funds to Ueno and concealing or downplaying its financial troubles, despite warnings of risky lending practices, while having financial ties to the bank.

Pena, who entered office in 2023, held a stake in the bank’s holding company until last year.

On Thursday, investigators raided his official residence in the capital, Asuncion. The prosecutor’s office said agents from the economic crimes unit were extracting data and gathering relevant information for the investigation.

Last week, Pena tried to step down as president, but Congress rejected his resignation, instead removing him from office through impeachment. Pena was arrested shortly after his removal.

The collapse of Ueno left customers locked out of their accounts, prompting huge protests across the country as thousands demanded accountability and their money back.

Prosecutors had been looking for missing funds and said on Friday that assets had been located abroad, although they did not specify in which countries. They had previously asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help locating the missing money.

“The necessary steps are under way to request that they be frozen,” prosecutor Francisco Cabrera told reporters.

Three former central bank officials were also arrested on Friday, accused of having known about Ueno’s issues since late last year.

The bank, which held more than $800m in public funds, grew quickly under Pena’s presidency from a financial technology company into a large firm handling state pensions and the accounts of several government entities.

The credit ratings agency Fitch has placed Paraguay’s sovereign rating on watch for a possible downgrade, which would make it more expensive for the government to borrow money.

On Thursday, the Central Bank said it had returned savings to more than 1.8 million people who had deposited money at the bank.

articles.title: Van Hollen calls to abolish Senate filibuster, rules out 2028 White House bid
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to be the next Senate majority leader, said Friday he wants to abolish the filibuster and ruled out a potential presidential run in 2028. Van Hollen, speaking to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, argued that legislation should pass the Senate…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to be the next Senate majority leader , said Friday he wants to abolish the filibuster and ruled out a potential presidential run in 2028.

Van Hollen, speaking to reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver, argued that legislation should pass the Senate with simple-majority votes and that the filibuster, which requires senators to muster 60 votes to pass most legislation, is “undemocratic.”

“My personal opinion is that we need democracy in the United States Senate and that means allowing ultimately a majority of senators to answer the call of the American people, so that means 51 votes,” Van Hollen said.

“My personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an antidemocratic — small ‘d’ — provision. It’s not in our Constitution. It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people,” he added.

“My view is we need to have a system where you have lots of debate, lots of debate, but at the end of the day, a majority reflecting the will of the people should be able to hold a view on an important measure,” he said. “This is an issue that I think we need to talk to the caucus about.”

Van Hollen said filibuster reform is especially important to pass what he called “democracy protection measures” to protect voting rights.

The Maryland senator, who formally announced Thursday his plan to challenge Schumer in a leadership race next month , also said he’s no longer considering a run for president in 2028.

Van Hollen told the Hill Nation Summit in July that he was actively exploring a presidential bid.

He visited New Hampshire, an important early presidential primary state, in June and September.

The debate over the future of the Senate filibuster has divided Senate Democrats.

Most Senate Democrats voted for a carve-out of the Senate’s filibuster rule in January 2022 to advance a democracy reform package that would establish voting protections for minority voters and put in place new campaign finance regulations.

The effort failed because then-centrist Sens. Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and Kyrsten Sinema (D-Ariz.) voted against weakening the filibuster rule. Both lawmakers have since left the Senate.

Van Hollen voted for filibuster reform nearly five years ago, and Schumer backed it as well.

But Schumer hasn’t said whether he would support scrapping the 60-vote threshold for most bills once Democrats seize control of the Senate next year with at least a 55-seat majority.

articles.body:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) said lawmakers who are warring with the opposite faction within the party had “missed the plot” of the midterm results during a major Democratic conference on Friday.

“I think Michigan gave a really clear demonstration that whatever side of the Democrats you feel like you’re on, that is not what is important right now, OK? Teamwork is what is important,” Slotkin told attendees at the What’s Next conference in Denver, saying people had “voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership.”

“If you have elected officials who are spending all their time fighting progressive versus moderate, then they have missed the plot of the election,” she continued. “That new generation is not going to be defined by progressive versus moderate. That new generation, quite simply, is are you on Team Fight or are you on Team Flight?”

Slotkin was among a number of high-profile Democrats who spoke at the party gathering in Colorado this week, which also included House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.).

Slotkin is also considered a potential White House candidate in the next presidential election, and she confirmed to reporters that she was “seriously” considering it.

“I want to be a part of the next generation of leaders going forward that does things differently and understands who they serve,” she told reporters after leaving the stage.

“I’m looking at it, I’m looking at it seriously, but I haven’t made any decisions,” she said.

Other colleagues and party members who are also looking at runs for the White House next cycle who attended the Democratic conference in Denver included Shapiro, Khanna and Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.).

articles.title: Carlos Cuerpo anuncia su primera medida como Ministro de Transportes tras el accidente de Urda: "Crear un libro blanco"
articles.standfirst: El ministro detalla en La Sexta el plan para recuperar la confianza ferroviaria
articles.summary: El ministro detalla en La Sexta el plan para recuperar la confianza ferroviaria
articles.body: El debate de actualidad económica e infraestructuras celebrado en La Sexta dejó intervenciones clave por parte del actual Ejecutivo. Durante su intervención inicial, Carlos Cuerpo quiso dedicar unas palabras de profundo respeto: "Buenas noches, un placer estar aquí y precisamente por ser este el tema de inicio, aún con más razón quería que mi primer mensaje fuera un mensaje de recuerdo para las víctimas, no solo del accidente de Urda, sino también de los otros dos accidentes mortales que hemos tenido este año, el de Adamuz y el de Gelida". En este sentido, y respondiendo a los interrogantes sobre la crisis del sector, el dirigente remarcó el rumbo de las actuaciones políticas: "Mi primera y más importante tarea es hacer que los españoles recobremos la confianza en nuestro sistema ferroviario, en nuestros trenes y esto tiene muchas dimensiones. La primera de ellas, sin duda, la dimensión de acompañamiento a las víctimas, como acabo de decir". A esto añadió que "hay un elemento también de inicio, de asunción de responsabilidades políticas, ya hemos pasado por ahí con la dimensión del ministro Puente". Asimismo, el responsable gubernamental recalcó la necesidad de transparencia y mejora continua: "Hay un elemento importantísimo también de avanzar en la investigación de las causas de los accidentes, incluido el de Adamuz, donde todavía no se ha terminado esa investigación, no solo para dar esa información, ese confort de qué ha pasado, si es que podemos llamarle confort a las víctimas, sino por lo menos esa necesidad de saber qué es lo que ha pasado y que se van a tomar las actuaciones necesarias como para que esto no vuelva a pasar". Profundizando en el plano operativo, se refirió al refuerzo de los protocolos: "Estamos también en el momento de reforzar todo lo necesario en materia de seguridad, actuaciones que tienen que ver con las indicaciones que nos da la agencia de seguridad ferroviaria, es decir, basándonos en los técnicos, las actuaciones que nos están diciendo además los indicatos, por ejemplo, los maquinistas, relacionadas, por ejemplo, con sus tiempos de trabajo, con la manera en la que ellos transmiten las incidencias al centro de control, y actuaciones en definitiva que tienen que ver con el refuerzo de la inversión donde de nuevo, esa inversión de dónde bebe, cuánto tenemos que invertir, pues lo que nos están diciendo los técnicos, que sea necesario para garantizar el mantenimiento de las condiciones óptimas". Finalmente, se anunció una iniciativa estructural a corto plazo: "Si me permite, y quería hacer también un anuncio en esta primera intervención, el lunes que viene vamos a crear una comisión técnica que se va a encargar en los próximos dos meses y para el próximo gobierno de crear, de generar un libro con libro blanco, es decir, un estudio con recomendaciones que salgan de un análisis exhaustivo de la situación actual del sistema ferroviario para que pueda ser, por ejemplo, por qué no, el germen de un pacto de Estado en materia de infraestructuras. Este análisis, este comité técnico estará compuesto por expertos, expertos del sector, pero también expertos de sectores que puedan aportar en materia de seguridad, como por ejemplo el aeronáutico". Para cerrar, en relación con el acuerdo con los colectivos profesionales, puntualizó que "las inversiones, de hecho, hubo un acuerdo la semana pasada firmado en este caso por el Consejo de ADIF, un acuerdo que bebe de las necesidades que han identificado los técnicos en este caso para el conjunto de nuestro sistema ferroviario, no solo las líneas convencionales, sino en particular también las líneas de AVE, que tiene en cuenta el grado de utilización, el grado también, por supuesto, o la edad de cada uno de estos de estas vías, porque no son las mismas, hemos tenido los últimos 40 años una inversión continuada y, por lo tanto, bebiendo de ese análisis técnico, de lo que necesita cada una de estas vías es como se ha calculado esa inversión y se va a pautar también las medidas o las obras necesarias para llevarla a cabo".

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) has “been with the Republicans” since Congress returned, after the Michigan Democrat endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the midterms.

“She’s been with the Republicans ever since she’s come back. So she’s been on the Republican side of the aisle,” Ocasio-Cortez said during an appearance on “The Don Lemon Show” that aired Thursday.

“This is just the epitome of a certain kind of transactional politics,” she added. “And it’s really sad.”

Stevens’s last-minute endorsement of the Republican candidate in Michigan’s competitive Senate race came after her feud with Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.). The feud, in the preceding days of the midterm elections, stemmed from a political advertisement tying Israel to high grocery prices in the U.S. Stevens released a statement saying incoming Michigan senator did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

Rogers lost to El-Sayed last week by more than 7 points, according to Decision Desk HQ . El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan was one of many Democratic wins in the midterm, with the party flipping GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Maine and Iowa.

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’s endorsement switch, telling reporters , “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.”

Stevens, who has defended her decision multiple times, tripled down on it following the midterm results, saying that her beliefs were “never measured by who would win at the ballot box.”

“I recognize that my decision has consequences. All important decisions do. I don’t regret it, but I am truly sorry that it upset some of my colleagues and people I care about personally,” she said.

Stevens faced significant backlash from her fellow Democrats following her decision, and members of her staff resigned shortly after . On Tuesday, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) advised her colleagues against removing Stevens from the House Democratic Caucus before the 120th Congress starts.

Ocasio-Cortez, in her recent interview, said this “isn’t just about endorsing the Republican … this is about a betrayal.”

“It showed that people were right in advocating for Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy in the primary over someone like Haley Stevens,” the New York Democrat added.

articles.title: Peltola vs. Sullivan not alone: 24 Alaska races still too close to call
articles.summary: Twenty-four races for federal and state office in Alaska remain uncalled more than a week after Election Day, including the closely watched U.S. Senate contest, as votes from across the expansive state trickle in. Roughly 84 percent of the expected vote has been reported statewide, according to The Hill’s election desk partner Decision Desk HQ…
articles.body:
Twenty-four races for federal and state office in Alaska remain uncalled more than a week after Election Day, including the closely watched U.S. Senate contest, as votes from across the expansive state trickle in.

Roughly 84 percent of the expected vote has been reported statewide, according to The Hill’s election desk partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Both federal races — for the Senate and House — are uncalled, as well as the gubernatorial race, four state Senate seats and 17 state House seats.

Candidates in Alaska must receive a majority of the vote under the state’s ranked choice voting system, in which voters rank their preferences on the ballot when casting their vote. If no candidate receives a majority, the last-place candidate is removed and their voters’ second preferences are reallocated to the remaining candidates. The process repeats until there is a majority.

A measure to repeal ranked choice voting failed for the second straight cycle , DDHQ projected Thursday.

In the Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by more than 2 points . Neither candidate has a majority of the vote, and the contest is likely to go to a runoff using ranked choice. Current estimations predict that Peltola is likely to win in the end, partly because she is already above 49 percent of the vote.

In the gubernatorial race, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins leads with just more than 50 percent of the vote. Three Republican candidates are splitting the rest of the vote three ways, none with more than 30 percent.

If Kreiss-Tomkins holds his vote share above 50 percent, he will win without the need for ranked choice voting. CNN projected him as the winner Thursday, a pickup for Democrats, but DDHQ has not yet called the race.

Alaska’s U.S. House race is also uncalled, but Rep. Nick Begich (R) leads the race against an independent challenger by more than 7 points. The Democrat in the race has just 7.5 percent of the vote.

Begich is at 48.6 percent of the vote, and DDHQ has projected that the race will go to a ranked choice voting instant runoff as the outstanding votes will not be enough to give Begich a majority. The incumbent remains the favorite given the gap between them.

Both chambers of Alaska’s Legislature are currently governed by a coalition of Democrats and moderate Republicans, with a few independents in the state House as well. The unconventional system makes control hard to predict from election results alone.

A full picture of what will happen in Alaska’s remaining races may take another week. Ranked choice voting tabulations will not take place until next Wednesday, when all vote counts are finalized. The counting process in Alaska takes several days because, given the state’s large geographic size, absentee ballots can be received up to 15 days after the election if they come from overseas.

articles.title: Son of ex-CIA chief Brennan charged with possessing sexual images of minors
articles.summary: The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was charged on Friday with “transportation of child pornography,” according to court documents.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was charged on Friday with “transportation of child pornography,” according to court documents and a U.S. law enforcement official. Kyle Brennan, of Warrenton, Virginia, was charged after an FBI review of his cellphone found 88 images that appeared to depict minor girls engaged in sexually explicit conduct, according to a criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. John Brennan is a longtime antagonist of President Donald Trump, and the Justice Department has been investigating the former CIA director for more than a year. A criminal complaint showed the investigation into Kyle Brennan began independently of the probe into his father, which has been dubbed by both proponents and detractors the “grand conspiracy” probe. The complaint said the investigation into the younger Brennan originated in 2024 with a tip to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, a child protection organization. Virginia authorities searched his home in July 2024, and the case was referred to the FBI last month, according to the criminal complaint. Kyle Brennan was under arrest, and made an initial court appearance in front of a federal magistrate. He was appointed a federal public defender. Kyle Brennan is being held in custody by the U.S. Marshals pending a detention hearing, which will take place next Wednesday. John Brennan, who led the CIA during Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, has been scrutinized as part of a wider probe examining whether law enforcement and intelligence officials violated Trump’s civil rights in prior investigations of the president. The conspiracy investigation has stalled in recent weeks following the resignations of senior prosecutors who had been overseeing it. No charges have so far been brought. John Brennan has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have accused prosecutors of improperly targeting Brennan at Trump’s direction. The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury last month, but his appearance was postponed after Joseph diGenova, a DOJ official who had been leading the investigation, resigned in September.

articles.title: Hassett denies report he is leaving White House
articles.summary: Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), pushed back Friday on a report that he will depart the Trump administration in the coming weeks. He told CNBC’s Eamon Javers through text that the report is “not true.” The White House also denied the report, writing on social platform X, “There is no…
articles.body:
Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), pushed back Friday on a report that he will depart the Trump administration in the coming weeks.

He told CNBC’s Eamon Javers through text that the report is “not true.”

The White House also denied the report, writing on social platform X , “There is no factual basis for this reporting. Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump’s economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump’s economic policies.”

Semafor reported earlier Friday that Hassett “has been inquiring about roles outside the administration” and that it had nothing to do with the GOP’s losses in the midterm elections.

Hassett, who chaired the Council of Economic Advisers during Trump’s first term, has helmed the NEC for the entirety of the president’s second term so far.

Former President Clinton established the council in 1993 , and its members advise the president on domestic and international economic policy issues.

The NEC director has vocally defended the president and his economic policies, including his tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, on CNBC, Fox Business and other cable channels. Days before the midterm elections , Hassett touted the economy and downplayed Americans’ concerns about the cost of living.

“All the things that have made the economy great, means that affordability crisis, it’s a myth,” Hassett said on Fox Business’s “Kudlow.”

Hassett also echoed Trump in criticizing former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for not backing further interest rate cuts the last two years. Hassett was one of multiple candidates considered to succeed Powell, with the president ultimately selecting Kevin Warsh.

Multiple administration officials have already left the White House since the midterms, which saw Democrats capture control of both chambers of Congress.

Stephen Miller replaced Susie Wiles as Trump’s chief of staff this week, and Richard Walters has also left his role as deputy chief of staff.

Four Justice Department officials have also departed since the midterms, including Harmeet Dhillon, who led the department’s Civil Rights Division .

articles.title: FAA grounds US flights nationwide after ‘communication issue’
articles.summary: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says federal aviation agency is ‘investigating the issue’.
articles.body:
The United States has grounded flights across the country after a “communication issue” impacted traffic control centres, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

“FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” Duffy wrote on social media.

The FAA said in a post on X that there had been a “temporary telecommunications outage” and that, as a precaution, all flights were being halted. International flights would be handled case by case, it added.

About 7,000 flights have been either delayed or cancelled due to the stop, according to FlightAware.

Some 4,042 flights were in the air, heading to US airports, when the ground stop was ordered, according to the tracking site Flightradar24.

The communication issue affects all 22 air route traffic control centres, which guide aircraft.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication that the ground stop was triggered by a threat to the US. “Everybody’s safe. The flights are accounted for,” he said. “This is not another 9/11.”

President Donald Trump had been briefed, he added.

Asked whether a planned rollout of a new AI tool meant to help air traffic controllers could be to blame, Mullin said officials had not ruled it out. “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We are going through that process,” he said.

The FBI does not believe a cyberattack or criminal activity caused the failure, Bloomberg reported, citing an official familiar with the matter.

The cited official said investigators were examining whether a software update could have caused the outage, though the cause had not been determined.

The disruption is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic control system, which has ⁠been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and ⁠shortages of controllers, as the FAA tries to replace ageing infrastructure.

Congress approved $12.5bn for the overhaul last year, and the Department of Transportation and the White House asked lawmakers on Friday for ⁠another $30.1bn.

This is the first nationwide US ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the September 11, 2001, attacks.

The FAA has not provided any indication of when the ground stop might be lifted.

articles.title: Bustinduy explota contra Figaredo por volver a poner en duda el sistema de pensiones: "Quiere hacer como en Paraguay"
articles.standfirst: El ministro acusa a Vox de querer privatizar las prestaciones tras cuestionar su sostenibilidad financiera
articles.summary: El ministro acusa a Vox de querer privatizar las prestaciones tras cuestionar su sostenibilidad financiera
articles.body: El debate sobre el futuro del sistema público de pensiones protagonizó uno de los momentos más tensos de la noche en La Sexta entre el ministro de Derechos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, y el diputado de Vox, José María Figaredo. El representante de la formación de ultraderecha abrió el enfrentamiento cuestionando la viabilidad del modelo actual y acusando al Ejecutivo de ponerlo en riesgo: "Este gobierno ha vaciado la caja de las pensiones, la deuda de España es cada día mayor, el déficit es cada día mayor y la sostenibilidad del sistema la están poniendo ustedes en peligro". Además, aseguró que, si llegan a gobernar, "garantizamos que las pensiones se cobrarán sea como sea". Ante estas afirmaciones, la moderadora del espacio, Ana Pastor, interpeló directamente a Figaredo para aclarar su postura respecto a la subida conforme al IPC. Tras responder el diputado con un escueto "por supuesto", la periodista le reprochó la contradicción con su actividad parlamentaria: "¿Y entonces por qué ha votado Vox en contra cuatro veces en el Congreso? Porque, explíquemelo, es que yo le pregunto, pero usted no contesta". Lejos de aclarar el sentido de su voto, Figaredo centró su réplica en señalar la llegada de extranjeros como el origen de los problemas económicos y de seguridad del país. "El grandísimo recorte de las pensiones es precisamente esa inmigración masiva que está socavando la viabilidad del sistema", afirmó el dirigente de Vox, vinculando también el fenómeno migratorio con el estancamiento salarial, el precio de los alquileres, el colapso de los servicios públicos y la inseguridad "en barrios como Usera, Nou Barris o Roquetas de Mar". En su turno de palabra, Pablo Bustinduy desmontó los argumentos de Figaredo defendiendo los datos de gestión del Gobierno de coalición. "El sistema de pensiones no solo es sostenible, sino que está garantizado, que hemos incrementado las pensiones un 30%, un 65% las no contributivas, y que las proyecciones a 2050 es que entonces España pagará lo que Italia está pagando ya hoy", subrayó el ministro para rechazar los augurios de quiebra. Bustinduy elevó el tono para denunciar las verdaderas intenciones detrás del modelo mixto defendido por José María Figaredo y su partido, recordando el fracaso de experiencias similares en el extranjero. "La razón por la que el señor Figaredo vota en contra en el Congreso, por la que quiere cambiar el sistema de pensiones para hacer como en Paraguay, es porque quieren hacer negocio, porque quieren privatizarlo, porque vienen a por ello", sentenció el titular de Derechos Sociales. Para cerrar su intervención, el representante del Frente Amplio reivindicó el carácter social de las prestaciones frente a los intentos de mercantilización. "En España hay 6 millones de personas que cobran menos del SMI como pensión, la inmensa mayoría mujeres, que son quienes han levantado este país, que han dado la vida para que hoy estemos aquí debatiendo", concluyó Bustinduy antes de reiterar que "estos señores lo que quieren hacer es privatizar el sistema".

articles.title: Newly elected Senate Democrats in the spotlight: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Kristen Welker dives into the first big decision facing the class of incoming Democratic senators.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Kristen Welker dives into the first big decision facing the class of incoming Democratic senators. Plus, Natasha Korecki explains why the midterm results could make Democrats’ 2028 presidential primary even more unwieldy. — Adam Wollner Newly elected Democrats in the spotlight as Senate leadership fight kicks off Analysis by Kristen Welker The first battle in the fight for the future of the Democratic Party will come next month, when Senate Democrats choose who their leader will be when they are in the majority next year. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced last night that he is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who has led the Democratic caucus in the chamber for a decade. And all eyes will be on the 13 newly elected Democrats joining the Senate. Many of the incoming freshman Democrats have been calling for change, but Schumer’s role in recruiting some of them and helping them win their races also looms large. Schumer’s supporters have likened ousting him to firing a baseball manager who just won the World Series. Two newly elected Democrats — Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota — have already said that they will support Van Hollen for majority leader. Four others — Maine’s Troy Jackson, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Illinois’ Juliana Stratton and Kansas’ Adam Hamilton — have publicly said they would oppose Schumer. “What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center, somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together, somebody who can bring the various factions in Democratic Party together, somebody with fresh ideas,” Hamilton told me on “Meet the Press” on Sunday. “So again, no disrespect for Chuck Schumer. Just, it feels like there’s time for — it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us. Just one incoming Democratic senator has said he will back Schumer: Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, who served three terms in the chamber before losing in 2024. Brown told NBC affiliate WCMH of Columbus that he was supporting Schumer “because I think he knows how to govern.” “He’s controversial, people think he hasn’t fought hard enough. But that’s up to people like me to make sure he does,” said Brown, whom Schumer encouraged to run. Another candidate Schumer heavily recruited, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, told CNN earlier this year that he has “made no commitments” about whom he would support as leader. Schumer also recruited former Rep. Mary Peltola, who is locked in a close race in Alaska that is too early to call, and it is not clear how she would vote if she wins. The other newly elected Democrats have been noncommittal. Iowa’s Josh Turek told me late last year that “the party needs change” and he would press candidates for leader on what they could do for his state. Texas’ James Talarico told CBS News after winning his race that he wants to meet with every leadership candidate. And New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas told CNN earlier this year that “it’s time for new voices” and he would wait to see who is running. The latest Democrat to flip a Senate seat — Mississippi’s Scott Colom — has expressed concerns about Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker of the House, both hailing from the same New York City borough. But he told MS NOW this morning that he is “not a no” on Schumer and he wants the next leader to prioritize the Deep South and “actually fight for rural America.” Ultimately, Schumer will need to secure majority support from the Senate Democratic caucus. After Van Hollen joined the race, Schumer expressed confidence, saying on X, “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.” Colom will join me to discuss all of this and more on “Meet the Press” this Sunday. Former Vice President Mike Pence, who recently suggested he could make another run for the White House, will also join for an exclusive interview. Blue wave ignites a wild, wide-open 2028 race By Natasha Korecki DENVER — Last week’s Democratic midterm sweep reached so far and so wide that it is already recasting conventional thinking about who can forge a winning path to the White House in 2028 — blowing the doors off of what was already expected to be a wide-open presidential race. There was something for everyone in Democratic politics. Moderates won, but so did progressives. Women scored victories in deep-red, statewide races. Candidates who didn’t have the most money won. Democrats won in the South and in rural states and districts. They scored big gains among young men and noncollege white voters. They also showed they could win back Hispanic voters. It has all scrambled the thinking for an upcoming 2028 presidential primary, potentially opening more paths to winning the Electoral College than Democrats have had or considered in years. That’s likely to lure even more White House hopefuls to join what is expected to be a crowded field. “It’s going to be the craziest, most wide-open primary,” said Brian Stryker, a longtime Democratic pollster. “I wouldn’t bet on anyone against the field. I wouldn’t say anyone has more than a 50% chance. I don’t know if anyone has more than a 20% chance.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Fate of Trump’s DC golf course makeover at East Potomac Park hangs before federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge is set to rule this weekend on whether the Trump administration can move forward with its planned closure of East Potomac Park and the historic public golf course there, with the judge signaling during a lengthy hearing Friday that she was not poised to allow it, at least for now. U.S.…
articles.body:
A federal judge is set to rule this weekend on whether the Trump administration can move forward with its planned closure of East Potomac Park and the historic public golf course there, with the judge signaling during a lengthy hearing Friday that she was not poised to allow it, at least for now.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes pushed back on claims from Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyers that the closure, which President Trump has said will happen Sunday, is meant to address urgent public safety risks and is separate from a broader proposed development project the president has been angling for.

“Why all of the sudden on Nov. 15 do these justify closing down the entire park?” Reyes asked Adam Gustafson, the principal deputy assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s Energy and Natural Resources Division.

The judge, who sits on the federal bench in D.C., is expected to rule by the end of Saturday.

Friday was the latest in a series of contentious, hours-long hearings over the project in recent months, in which the judge, who was appointed by former President Biden, has frequently scolded DOJ officials for seemingly misrepresenting the plans as different from the president’s public comments.

“I’m trying to figure out which iteration of me not paying attention to the president I’m supposed to go with today,” Reyes said Friday.

The judge previously said she intended to tap former U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jessie Liu to investigate whether Trump administration lawyers may have “ committed ethical violations ” during the ongoing litigation.

“That does not mean in any way, shape or form that I think anything untoward has happened,” Reyes said. “It only means that I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there’s been fire.”

In turn, the Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and demanded she recuse from the case. She has refused to do so .

The judge has already barred the Trump administration from cutting any more trees at East Potomac Park unless they pose an imminent risk to public safety. Even then, Reyes said the administration must provide 24-hour notice.

The Trump administration has appealed that ruling to the D.C. Circuit.

The future of East Potomac Park has been uncertain for months, following the National Park Service’s termination of its lease with the National Links Trust, the local nonprofit that had operated the courses there since the coronavirus pandemic.

Months after Trump, in a post on Truth Social, proposed a design for a new course, the department abruptly removed hundreds of trees from the park as confused golfers played just feet away.

A preservationist group and local golfers who are suing to stop the redevelopment also want Reyes to block the park from closing Sunday, when the National Links Trust (NLT) has said it would cede operational control of the courses there.

“It’s not, as you were saying earlier, just a massive coincidence that NLT suddenly up and decided to leave as of the very same day that the president directed defendants to close the park,” argued Catherine Carroll, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs.

The Trump administration terminated a lease with the NLT last year, and the president has said the property would close this month so construction on an 18-hole championship-length facility can begin.

The new proposed course, which would be designed by famed architect Tom Fazio, calls for a championship-level facility that would stretch more than 8,000 yards from the back tees, making it one of the largest in the country.

Critics from around the golf world have argued such a design will reduce accessibility for amateur golfers who have long been able to play at East Potomac, which has primarily catered to beginners and more casual golfers, at an affordable price.

The judge polled the courtroom early into the hearing, asking attendees to raise their hands if they had “strong views” about the redesign. The “vast majority” did, she noted.

Gustafson said the Fazio concept is not final, and the Interior Department could still “change its mind” pending public feedback.

Major questions about the project’s feasibility and cost remain.

A damaged seawall, which has been in poor condition since the Obama administration, leads to frequent flooding at the park and will cost hundreds of millions of dollars to repair.

The government has so far provided few details on where financing for the seawall repair would come from, while attorneys for the administration pointed to its condition in arguing the peninsula needs to be closed off to the public.

Reyes drilled down on the government’s assertions Friday, questioning what changed that required an immediate closure when deteriorating conditions have been documented for more than a decade.

“Just days after 30,000-plus people ran around Ohio Drive, it is an emergent situation,” she said, referring to the Marine Corps marathon last month that went directly around Hains Point. “So, tell me what happened.”

Gustafson deflected when faced with similar lines of questioning throughout the hearing, pointing several times only to safety and the lack of an operator as justification for the imminent closure.

Reyes called the latter a “self-inflicted” issue, comparing it to a situation in which a person starts a fire at their home and then tries to recoup insurance money.

“You’re the one who set the house on fire,” she told the DOJ.

articles.title: Angie Nixon fires back at Carville: ‘He needs to go retire’
articles.summary: Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), who lost to GOP incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in last week’s midterm elections, called Democratic strategist James Carville a “racist” in a Thursday night interview, adding he should “go retire.” “That man is a racist,” Nixon told former MS NOW commentator Joy Reid during an appearance on “The Joy…
articles.body:
Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), who lost to GOP incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in last week’s midterm elections, called Democratic strategist James Carville a “racist” in a Thursday night interview, adding he should “go retire.”

“That man is a racist,” Nixon told former MS NOW commentator Joy Reid during an appearance on “The Joy Reid Show .”

“The way in which he talks and how he has continued to downplay the work that I was able to do and the work that other folks have been able to do, other Black candidates, is just really mad disrespectful,” she added. “He needs to go retire and stop being disrespectful.”

Nixon’s remarks came after Carville, during a conversation with Gen Z for Change founder Aidan Kohn-Murphy on the Democratic strategist’s “ Politics War Room ” podcast, called Nixon “a uniquely uninspiring Senate candidate.”

“You may like her politics. She was not a good statewide candidate. She was not a good fit for the state of Florida,” Carville said.

The Florida Democrat directly addressed Carville’s postmidterm commentary, saying, “You were very disrespectful. And, you know, it doesn’t matter if you don’t like me, I didn’t drag anyone down.”

“James Carville, your analysis is whack. It is not truthful and it is rooted in the white supremacy that continued to run this country,” Nixon added.

Florida is one of the few historically red states in which Republicans maintained their stronghold on Election Day, as Democrats secured sweeping victories across the country — claiming both congressional chambers and flipping GOP-held seats in states like Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas, among others.

Nixon lost the Senate race to her GOP opponent by a little less than 3 points, according to Decision Desk HQ , The Hill’s election results partner. The state’s gubernatorial race also swung in the Republicans’ favor, with Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) defeating Democrat David Jolly by a little more than 1 point.

Earlier, Nixon called the contest a “ missed opportunity ” for Democrats.

“If we want to continue to profess that we care about Black people and Hispanic communities, then we need to invest in them,” Nixon said on “The Don Lemon Show” earlier this week. “Black women, especially Black people, are seen as the backbone of the party, and so they need to not only invest … in our labor so to speak, they need to really invest in our leadership.”

articles.title: Juan Bravo contra el relato fiscal de Bustinduy sobre el impuesto a los ricos: "¿Saben cuántos ganan más de 60.000 €? Ni el 6%"
articles.standfirst: El representante del PP en el debate a cuatro de LaSexta denuncia la subida masiva de impuestos a las rentas medias en España
articles.summary: El representante del PP en el debate a cuatro de LaSexta denuncia la subida masiva de impuestos a las rentas medias en España
articles.body: El plató de La Sexta acogió un debate económico centrado en la fiscalidad, los servicios públicos y la distribución de la riqueza, con un enfrente directo entre el ministro de Derechos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, y el representante del Partido Popular, Juan Bravo. La tensión escaló cuando Bustinduy criticó duramente el modelo económico actual y argumentó que el sistema extrae recursos de la clase trabajadora. Según el propio Bustinduy, esto sucede mediante el encarecimiento de la vida y el deterioro de lo público: "Está extrayendo a través de la vivienda y del desmantelamiento de los servicios públicos, porque cada vez que el Partido Popular te obliga a contratar un seguro médico privado, una plaza privada en una escuelita, en una residencia, de esta restando tu salario en directo, porque el salario de los trabajadores también son los servicios públicos". El ministro continuó su intervención cargando contra la brecha fiscal entre grandes corporaciones y autónomos, señalando que los beneficios se concentran en pocas manos mientras se debilita el estado del bienestar: "Aquí el problema es que las grandes empresas que se están forrando en España pagan menos que una PYME. Aquí el problema es que las rentas patrimoniales pagan menos que las rentas del trabajo en este país". Asimismo, denunció que la presión fiscal nacional se mantiene distanciada de las principales economías del entorno comunitario: "La media, la presión fiscal en España sigue tres puntos por debajo de la media europea, estamos 8 puntos por debajo de Francia. 160.000 millones de euros, lo que podríamos hacer en términos de redistribución y de estado del bienestar con eso". Frente a estos argumentos, intervinieron las alusiones directas al principal partido de la oposición y rápidamente tomó la palabra Juan Bravo para rebatir los datos del Ejecutivo aportando cifras sobre los declarantes del impuesto sobre la renta: "Cuando el Sr. Bustinduy les cuenta esto, yo les quiero contar un dato objetivo de la agencia tributaria. En España, presentar la renta, y recuerden que los que ganan menos de 24.000 no tienen por qué presentarla, pero cojamos solo los que lo han presentado, 24,6 millones de personas. ¿Saben de esas personas cuántos de ustedes ganan más de 100.000... más de 60.000€? Más de 60.000, 1,6. No llega ni al 6%. La mayoría están entre 20.000 y 60.000€". El representante popular reprochó además al bloque de gobierno que la carga tributaria recaiga constantemente sobre los mismos perfiles socioeconómicos: "Y a esos es donde está la recaudación y a esos en los que estos señores os han subido 100 veces los impuestos, más de 100 veces. Y su propuesta, la estaréis escuchando, es volver a subir los impuestos...". En ese instante, Bustinduy interrumpió para matizar a quiénes deben dirigirse las cargas impositivas: "¡A los ricos! Subir los impuestos a los ricos para financiar los servicios públicos de todos. No eliminar el impuesto al patrimonio, no eliminar los impuestos a las herencias, no bajar impuestos a las grandes fortunas, no eliminar el impuesto a las grandes fortunas, que es lo que quiere hacer el Partido Popular para perdonarle los impuestos a los de arriba...". El debate se cerró con una última puntualización de Juan Bravo para insistir en el volumen real de contribuyentes afectados por los tramos medios: "¡Recuerde! ¡Veintitrés millones entre 20 y 60!". De este modo, el enfrentamiento televisivo puso de manifiesto dos modelos fiscales radicalmente opuestos de cara a la gestión de los recursos públicos en el país.

articles.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
articles.summary: Work requirements were set to go into effect on Jan. 1 for many able-bodied adults who receive Medicaid, which could have left millions without health insurance.
articles.body: The federal government on Friday announced a six-month delay in enforcing a Medicaid work requirement — a central provision in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” that experts said would lead millions of Americans to lose health coverage. The requirement still technically starts on Jan. 1, but under new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, states that choose not to enforce it won’t be held accountable until at least July 1. The move is a striking turn for an administration that has spent months defending the policy against criticism from state officials and healthcare advocates who warned that the rollout was moving too quickly and that people who should be eligible for Medicaid would lose coverage because of the additional red tape and paperwork. CMS called the six-month window a “hold harmless” period, and the delay is optional. States that choose to take advantage of this period will still start checking on Jan. 1 whether Medicaid enrollees are working, volunteering or in school or whether they qualify for an exemption. But until July, no one in those states will lose coverage for failing to meet the requirements. “States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term,” said Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at CMS. The White House declined to comment. Some states have already moved forward with implementing the work requirements. In Nebraska, which launched the work requirements May 1, over 1,000 people have lost coverage or been denied benefits because of the new rules, according to state figures through August. The Medicaid work requirement was a cornerstone of Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” a massive tax and spending package that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy through tax breaks while slashing the social safety net for vulnerable Americans. Millions of Americans are expected to lose health coverage and food assistance as a result of the law, the signature domestic legislation of Trump’s second term. The law requires many able-bodied adults under the age of 65 to prove they work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours a month to keep Medicaid, which provides health coverage for low-income and disabled Americans. The Trump administration argues the requirement and other provisions in the law encourage work, reduce waste and protect government benefit programs for those who need them. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work requirements alone would leave 5.3 million more people uninsured by 2034 and would save the federal government $317 billion, part of nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts in the law. Pressure on the administration to delay the requirement had been building for months. Five Democratic governors last month asked Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to postpone the implementation, saying that state agencies weren’t ready. And a federal judge last month blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a portion of the requirement related to medically frail people, saying it could lead some to wrongly lose coverage. The delay comes a little more than a week after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on a promise to reverse the GOP’s cuts to healthcare and food assistance. “Millions of people’s health care is at risk because of the Republican reconciliation law’s work requirement, as states scramble to implement on a rushed timeline & respond to shifting federal requirements,” Sarah Lueck, vice president for health policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said in a post on X. “Today’s news lets states delay the harm.”

articles.body:
U.S. poised to lose measles elimination status

The United States is on the brink of losing its measles elimination status after more than 25 years. Losing measles elimination status would be mostly symbolic, but it marks a step back for public health .

According to the latest release of data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there are more than 5,400 confirmed measles infections nationwide, more than twice that of last year’s.

New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have all reported their first measles-related deaths in decades this year, with 10 deaths reported by the states.

The CDC’s total currently only reflects six deaths, with the agency having switched from relying on states to official death certificate data, which takes longer to confirm.

Elimination status means that there have been no sustained instances of measles transmission for 12 months or more. The rising infections have been driven by declining vaccination rates ; the national MMR vaccination rate in school-age children reached a new low of 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, with 39 states reporting rates that fall below the 95% target threshold.

To lose elimination status, measles must be spreading for 12 months or more, which passed in January of this year.

The U.S. first achieved measles elimination status in 2000 , with infection rates falling significantly after the two-dose measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was adopted at the national level in 1989.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has been reviewing the nation’s status this week, and the result is all but certain. Canada lost its own measles elimination status one year ago and has since been working with PAHO on regaining it.

In a statement on Thursday, the Infectious Disease Society of America called the formal loss of the country’s elimination status a “tragedy.”

“The expected loss of America’s status as having eradicated measles will be a tragedy because it reflects the preventable loss of human lives. It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026,”

articles.title: Rubio, off script, leans into inspiring vision for America as 2028 speculation grows
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio promoted an inspirational view of the United States during remarks at a conservative law conference Friday, invoking the image of a country where an ambitious attitude binds Americans — striving toward living up to the founding ideals Rubio’s off-script remarks, which followed a keynote address during the annual conference of…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio promoted an inspirational view of the United States during remarks at a conservative law conference Friday, invoking the image of a country where an ambitious attitude binds Americans — striving toward living up to the founding ideals

Rubio’s off-script remarks, which followed a keynote address during the annual conference of The Federalist Society, provided a window into how a potential presidential campaign may rally voters.

Rubio has dismissed the notion he’s planning to leave the administration early to launch a presidential campaign. But Republican voters are in favor of his running in 2028, with 45 percent rating him as an excellent candidate, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll . Vice President Vance was not far behind with 43 percent.

Rubio was relaxed, joking and encouraging while responding to questions from law students at the Friday evening conference in Washington, D.C. The conservative legal society served as a key pipeline for staffing President Trump’s second term and implementing an expansive view of executive power.

The secretary encouraged one student to focus on the value of human dignity and caring for the less fortunate when asked how a Christian attorney should respond when pressured to leave faith at the door.

“Remember, I did land-use and zoning,” Rubio joked of his law practice, moving seamlessly between humor and sincerity — demonstrating skills he’s honed throughout an over two-decade political career.

On Iran, Rubio said U.S. economic pressure is replacing the need for military action — echoing Trump’s downplaying of renewed strikes on the country — but did not provide a vision for an offramp.

“It’s hard, it’s not easy, and it’s difficult, and oftentimes it inflicts pain, economic pain, and otherwise. So, we recognize that, but victory is they can never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

Rubio gave a lighter touch to hot-button culture issues, where the Trump administration has sought to overhaul how America’s history is presented related to slavery, racism and imperialism.

“I never said our history’s perfect, I said our history is better than anybody else’s,” Rubio said in response to a question on how to instill “love for the values of our country” for the next generation.

Rubio said, “All the great justice movements in our history” — the abolition of slavery, the end of segregation and women gaining the right to vote — was a “demand that we live up to our founding principle.”

The secretary’s off-script remarks served as a contrast to a more bullish and confrontational prepared speech, where Rubio accused practitioners of international law of making an effort to weaken the United States — drawing applause when highlighting the administration’s sanctioning of the International Criminal Court.

“They think they have the right to rule over everyone,” he said.

“If they are foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees, our answer will be the same as the Roman general Pompey… ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

That line unexpectedly drew laughter, causing the secretary to adlib into a joke about how Pompey was not politically correct.

The secretary’s prepared remarks on Friday echoed a speech he delivered last month in Athens, where he sought to make a case for America’s unrestrained ambition and right to conquest.

The October speech also drew attention as possibly laying the groundwork for a 2028 presidential run. The scene was stunning — the ancient Acropolis in the background lit by the setting Mediterranean sun. But the speech was overshadowed by a host of controversies engulfing then-U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Trump fired her shortly after Rubio’s remarks, responding to negative press that Guilfoyle sought to trade access to the administration in exchange for cash.

Rubio poked fun at Democrats’ resounding midterm victory and pledges by the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif), to investigate allegations of corruption and threats to national security.

“There was a congressman who said we all needed to lawyer up, so here we are,” he quipped.

articles.body:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is projected to win the Alaska governor’s office , becoming the first Democrat to win the office in more than 20 years, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, defeated Republican Bernadette Wilson and two others in the Last Frontier’s four-way, ranked-choice general election.

DDHQ projected the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, who took 50.8 percent of the vote over Wilson’s 28.1 percent, with 90 percent of ballots counted as of 11:57 p.m. EST Friday.

Democrat Tom Begich, a member of Alaska’s storied Begich family, had advanced from this summer’s primary, but dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins to help clear a path to Democratic victory.

Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson (R) and former Attorney General Treg Taylor (R) were also in the running, raising concerns that the trio of Republicans would split the party’s vote amid voter skepticism about the ranked-choice system.

Kreiss-Tomkins, who was endorsed by GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), also led in fundraising and polls as the race entered its home stretch.

The 37-year-old is on track to be sworn in as the youngest governor in the state’s history and the first Democrat to win the seat since 1998 —- ending the GOP’s winning streak that was interrupted by independent Bill Walker’s lone gubernatorial term in 2014.

Kreiss-Tomkins will replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who won reelection by more than 25 percentage points in 2022.

Cook Political Report shifted the race from Republicans’ domain to “toss-up” territory in September, then to a surprising “lean Democrat” label in October.

The Alaska race was one of five potential flips for Democrats in the three-dozen gubernatorial races on Tuesday’s ballot, according to forecasts from DDHQ a week before the election.
